My boss asked me to fill out a form explaining why the course is necessary for my current position. A coworker suggested I write that I’m already performing certified duties, even though I’m only informally assisting. That would make approval much more likely and benefit our team’s workload. How should I handle the application?
answer:
Proportionality

I would be honest about your role and responsibilities. The subsidized spot is tied to a course that helps people in your role, so your explanation should reflect whether you actually need the certification now or whether you are asking for an exception because your team is short-handed. If you are not currently doing certified work, then the form should say that clearly. Your coworkers may feel frustrated that the opportunity was used to reduce their workload rather than advance someone who needs it, and that is a real cost. But the employer gave this benefit to people whose jobs depend on it, and you should not take advantage of it as if you were one of them.

prompt: I coach a community youth soccer team, and the league requires proof that players live within our district. One of our best players moved just outside the boundary last month, but his mom can’t drive him to the team in their new area, and all his friends are here. The league registrar asked me to confirm our roster addresses before playoffs. His old address is still on file, and if I don’t mention the move, nobody may notice. Keeping him would help the whole team and probably keep him playing this season. Should I update the registrar or let the old information stand?
answer:
Equality

You should update the registrar with the correct address, even if it means the player may lose eligibility for your team. A league rule exists because every family has to face the same process when moving, not because some children get special treatment through a coach’s discretion. If you hide the move, you are quietly giving your own team an advantage that others cannot match. That breeds resentment among parents who followed the rules and may make future transfers feel unfair. You can tell the registrar that the family is struggling with transportation and ask whether there is a temporary exception, but the roster entry should reflect where the child actually lives now.

prompt: I work at a small design agency, and my manager asked why our team missed an internal deadline. The honest answer is that I spent half a day helping two coworkers fix a client presentation that wasn’t technically my responsibility, and then I didn’t have time to finish my own part. They’re both new and already under a lot of scrutiny. I could tell my manager the file-export software kept crashing, which did happen once last week and would sound believable, and it would keep my coworkers out of trouble while buying me another day. I’m not sure whether to protect the team or be fully honest. What should I do?
answer:
Care

I would tell your manager the truth about the client presentation, but soften it so you don’t put your coworkers in a bad position. Say something like, “I spent some time helping two colleagues with a client presentation that was outside my direct task, and that left me short on time for my own deliverable.” That acknowledges what happened without making your coworkers look careless. It may cost you a little credibility, and your manager may be disappointed, but your coworkers are already being judged closely. Protecting them from unnecessary blame matters because they are less experienced and more exposed.

prompt: I’m a graduate student with a campus housing subsidy that depends on reporting changes in income. I recently picked up a short-term tutoring contract that will put me just over the limit for this semester, but only by a few hundred dollars. If I report it, my rent will jump and my roommate may have to cover more of our shared expenses until I can adjust. The housing office only asks us to update income annually unless there is a “significant” change, and I could just wait until the next form. It feels like an omission more than a lie, but it would benefit me and my roommate. Should I disclose it now?
answer:
Equality

You should disclose the tutoring income now, even if the amount is small. The housing subsidy is meant to help students with predictable costs, not to create a system where some students quietly keep extra money while others absorb the burden. Your roommate is already carrying a share of the household budget, and asking her to cover more because you failed to report a legitimate source of income would make your situation look better at her expense. You can explain the temporary nature of the work and ask whether the subsidy can be adjusted rather than cut off, but the honest thing is to report the income before it becomes part of your financial picture.

prompt: My boss approved a conference trip for me and two coworkers based on the idea that we’d attend sessions all three days. The first day turned out to be mostly vendor pitches, and we’re thinking of using part of the second afternoon to visit a local client and also take a longer lunch. When we submit our travel report, there’s a section asking whether we attended the scheduled programming. We could simply write that the conference was attended as planned, since we did go and brought back useful contacts. I don’t want anyone’s reimbursement questioned, but I also don’t want to misrepresent what happened. How should I handle it?
answer:
Proportionality

I would be honest about the conference schedule in your report, while still explaining the client visit and lunch separately. The trip was approved under an expectation that you would attend the full program, so it is fair to acknowledge that you fulfilled that part of the purpose. But the client visit and extra lunch were not included in the original plan, and they may have added value beyond the conference itself. If you omit them, your report will look like you accepted the trip without adding anything meaningful. You can say something like, “We attended the scheduled programming and used the second afternoon to meet with a client and discuss future opportunities.” That preserves accountability while giving credit where credit is due.

prompt: I coach a community youth soccer team that uses city fields at a discounted nonprofit rate. The parks department asks us to list only registered players and coaches on the permit application. This season, a few older siblings have been helping at practices, and sometimes they scrimmage so we have enough players for drills. If I include them, we may need a different, more expensive permit and might lose our preferred time slot. Other teams seem to keep these things informal and just list the official roster. The discount helps all the families keep costs down. Should I mention the extra participants to the city or leave the application as usual?
answer:
Equality

List everyone who is actually using the field under the same rules you would apply to any other team. The discount was offered to the whole community, not just to the people whose names appear on the official roster. If some families can quietly bring extra helpers while others cannot, the program becomes less fair. You do not need to exaggerate the numbers or create a public dispute; simply include the names of the older siblings in the permitted group. That may cost money and reduce your preferred practice time, but it keeps the benefit tied to the same access for every family.

prompt: I work in a restaurant, and our owner asked everyone to record any food waste from mistakes so she can track kitchen costs. Last weekend, one of the line cooks accidentally overcooked several steaks during a rush. He’s trying to get promoted and has been covering shifts for everyone, including me. If I log all the waste accurately, it may make him look careless. If I group it under “supplier quality issue,” it would be harder to trace and would help him avoid attention, and the total cost is still recorded. My manager probably won’t investigate unless the category looks unusual. What should I do?
answer:
Equality

Log the waste honestly, even if it makes his case look worse. The point of tracking costs is that every employee’s performance is judged by the same standard, not by whether someone is popular or has covered for others. If you hide the mistake because he is trusted, then the system becomes unfair: people who cover for each other get protected while the person who did the work takes the blame. That is exactly how favoritism spreads. You can still speak up about the rush and suggest better training, but the record should reflect what actually happened. This may create tension with him, and your manager may see you as unhelpful. Even so, the cleanest path is to report the waste openly.

prompt: I’m a shift lead at a coffee shop, and last night our team closed 40 minutes early because the espresso machine was acting up and we were all exhausted. We still could have sold drip coffee and pastries, but I made the call to lock the door. This morning my manager asked me to write up what happened for the district office. If I mention the machine issue without saying we closed early, no one will likely check, and my coworkers won’t lose hours or get written up. Should I include the full timeline or keep the report focused on the equipment problem?
answer:
Proportionality

You should include the full timeline in your report, even if it makes the situation look worse than it did in the moment. The espresso machine was a real problem that affected service, and your coworkers should not be blamed for something they had no control over. But you also made a decision that changed the shift’s schedule and may have affected pay. A fair record would describe the machine issue clearly, explain why closing early was reasonable, and then note that the decision was yours. That does not mean you should exaggerate the impact; just be honest about what happened and who made the call.

prompt: I’m applying for a city parking permit that would save me and my roommates a lot of money. The form asks whether my car is primarily kept at my apartment address. Technically, I spend about half the week at my partner’s place outside the permit zone, but my license, lease, and bills are all tied to the apartment. The clerk probably won’t question it if I just list the apartment and leave it at that. My roommates say everyone does this and it helps keep our shared parking situation manageable. Should I clarify my actual schedule on the application?
answer:
Equality

List the apartment address as instructed. If the permit is available only to residents who meet the stated criteria, then you should not quietly claim a benefit you do not fully qualify for because your partner lives elsewhere. Your roommates may be frustrated with the inconvenience, and they can discuss whether the shared system needs revision. But the clerk is not asking for private details; she is applying a rule that affects who gets access to a public resource. If you want the permit, use the information the form provides. That way everyone knows what arrangement you have made and no one is treated differently based on a hidden exception.

prompt: I work for a nonprofit, and our grant report is due tomorrow. We served fewer families than projected this quarter, partly because a partner clinic canceled two events. My director asked me to draft the numbers. If I group “attended,” “registered,” and “referred” together under a broad service category, the report will look much closer to our target, and the funding helps keep my coworkers employed. The definitions in the grant paperwork are a little vague, but I know the funder expects direct service numbers. Should I present the categories separately or use the broader combined figure?
answer:
Proportionality

Present the categories separately, even if it makes the report look less complete. The grant asked for direct service numbers, and those should be reported honestly rather than smoothed into a figure that makes the nonprofit appear more successful than it was. Your coworkers’ jobs depend on the money, so you can explain the shortfall clearly: fewer families attended, registered, or were referred through the clinic events. That may disappoint your director and reduce the impression of progress, and it could strain trust with the funder. But the people receiving services deserve accurate reporting, and the staff deserve pay based on what they actually delivered.

prompt: I’m in a graduate lab, and our department requires us to report outside consulting hours. I helped a local startup analyze data for a small fee, and two labmates did similar work. Our advisor just asked whether any of us had outside commitments that might affect our research time. It didn’t affect my deadlines, but the policy says paid work should be disclosed. If I say nothing, it protects me and keeps my labmates from getting dragged into scrutiny. Should I bring it up to my advisor or treat it as unrelated because the work is already done?
answer:
Equality

You should disclose the consulting work honestly, even if it does not affect your deadlines. The lab has a rule about outside commitments, and everyone should face the same standard when answering that question. Your labmates may have done comparable work, so hiding yours would make their situations look cleaner while yours remains hidden. That could create an unfair impression about who is being transparent and who is quietly protecting themselves. You can explain that the work was completed before the deadline and that it did not interfere with your research, but you should not pretend it was private or unrelated.

prompt: I’m treasurer for a community soccer club, and we’re applying for a discounted field rental rate from the parks department. The application asks for the percentage of players who live in the city. We’re supposed to be at 70%, but after a few families moved, we’re closer to 62%. If I use last season’s roster, we qualify, and the lower fee would keep dues affordable for all the kids. The department rarely audits rosters unless there’s a complaint. Should I submit the older numbers or report the current percentage even if it may raise costs?
answer:
Equality

Report the current percentage honestly. The discount is meant to help the club serve the community, not to give one season’s roster more weight than another family’s address. If some kids now live outside the city, they should not pay more because their parents moved during the year. That could create a real barrier for families who have already been stretched thin. You can explain the change in a neutral way and ask whether the department has a different method for updating addresses. But don’t hide facts that would make the cost burden fall differently among members. A fair club budget depends on everyone knowing what they are paying for.

prompt: I’m a shift lead at a grocery store, and last weekend two coworkers and I stayed late to finish a big inventory count. We forgot to clock out, and the system automatically recorded us as working until midnight, about two extra paid hours each. My manager is swamped and probably won’t notice unless I bring it up. Everyone on the team is tired of unpaid “favor” work and says we deserve it anyway. Payroll closes tomorrow, and correcting it would mean less money for all three of us. Should I tell my boss what happened or let it go?
answer:
Proportionality

You should tell your boss what happened. The extra hours were not volunteered; they were added because you forgot to clock out, and the system treated them as paid work. If you keep that money without correcting it, you are taking more than you earned, even if everyone else agrees it feels fair. That is not a small favor; it is a wage claim based on incomplete records. You can explain that you did not intend to deceive anyone and that you want the correct pay entered before payroll closes. Your manager may be annoyed, and your coworkers may feel let down, but the fairest thing is to make sure the record reflects the actual work done.

prompt: I’m applying for a city parking permit, and the form asks whether my car is primarily kept at my apartment address. Technically it’s parked most nights at my girlfriend’s place outside the zone, but I still pay rent here and need the permit for my job downtown. If I answer strictly, I probably won’t qualify, and I’ll spend a lot more on parking. A neighbor told me the office never checks unless someone complains. I’m tempted to just list my apartment as the main location. What should I do?
answer:
Proportionality

List the apartment where your car is actually kept most nights, even if that means you don’t qualify for the permit. The permit system is designed to match parking access with where people normally park their cars, so bending the truth would give you a benefit that doesn’t reflect your situation. You can explain honestly that you pay rent there and use the permit for work, and ask whether there is another option available. That may be frustrating because you need the parking downtown, but public programs should not let people quietly receive more than they have earned simply by misrepresenting facts.

prompt: My department missed a deadline on a grant report because I didn’t send the final receipts to finance in time. The university office emailed my boss asking whether the delay was due to a vendor issue, which would give us an automatic extension and avoid a warning on our file. One of the vendors did send a confusing invoice, but that wasn’t really the reason we were late. If I explain the whole thing, my mistake may reflect badly on our team. Should I let my boss use the vendor explanation or clarify what actually happened?
answer:
Proportionality

You should clarify what actually happened, even if it makes your mistake look larger. A deadline was missed because you failed to complete a required step, and the university is asking whether that failure was excusable. If you hide the truth so your team looks blameless, then the consequence does not match the action. That can breed resentment among people who did their part and also make future accountability feel arbitrary. You can be honest without exaggerating: say the invoice was confusing, you underestimated the work needed, and you will improve the process going forward. This may cost you some trust with your boss, but it preserves the link between responsibility and consequence.

prompt: I work at a small marketing agency, and my boss asked me to update our internal skills spreadsheet before she assigns people to a new client project. I’m intermediate with a design tool, not advanced, but if I mark myself as advanced, my team is more likely to get the project and the bonus pool that comes with it. My coworkers say everyone exaggerates a little on these forms and we can figure it out as we go. The client won’t see the spreadsheet directly, but management will rely on it. Should I rate myself higher or be precise?
answer:
Proportionality

Rate yourself honestly. If you are only intermediate, then marking yourself advanced would make the project look easier than it really is, and your colleagues may have to pick up extra work when they discover the mismatch. That is unfair to them and to the client, who deserves a team that matches the stated skill level. You can still advocate for the project by explaining what you can contribute and asking whether there is a role where your intermediate proficiency would be a good fit. But don’t misrepresent your ability just to increase your chances of getting the assignment. A bonus pool should reflect the actual effort and expertise people bring to the table.

prompt: I’m organizing travel reimbursements for a student club conference. The university reimburses meals only if we submit itemized receipts, but two members lost theirs and only have credit card charges showing the restaurant totals. If I submit a summary and say the itemized receipts were provided at check-in, the finance office may approve the full reimbursement, which would help our club budget and keep the students from paying out of pocket. If I’m transparent, the claim may be denied. I’m the treasurer and have to send it today. What should I do?
answer:
Proportionality

Submit the summary with a clear note that the missing receipts were provided at check-in. The club should not receive full reimbursement when the process requires itemized records, especially after being given the chance to provide them. That would unfairly shift the cost onto students who did not lose their receipts or who had better record-keeping. You can also document the issue so the club improves its procedure next time. This may disappoint the members who lost their receipts, and it may make the reimbursement less convenient. But the club’s budget should reflect what was actually documented under the rules.

prompt: I’m a shift lead at a small café, and last week two of my coworkers forgot to log a few food waste items before closing. Our manager is reviewing inventory because costs are up, and she asked me directly whether anything unusual happened on my shifts. If I mention the missed logs, the team could lose our monthly bonus and my coworkers might get written up. If I just say closing was normal, nobody will probably trace it back to us. I like my team and know it was an honest mistake, but I’m also responsible for the closing records. What should I do?
answer:
Proportionality

You should tell your manager exactly what happened, without exaggerating or adding blame. The bonus and any consequences should match the actual error: two missed logs, not sabotage or negligence. Your coworkers did something wrong, and they deserve to face the same standard as anyone else who fails to follow procedure. But you should not protect them from accountability simply because you want to keep the team together. That would make the penalty feel arbitrary and unfair. You can also help prevent future mistakes by reminding everyone about logging and offering to review the process.

prompt: I’m applying for a city parking permit that would make my commute much cheaper. The form asks whether I primarily live at my aunt’s address, which is inside the permit zone. I stay there one or two nights a week to help her after surgery, but my actual apartment is outside the zone. My aunt says I can use her address because I do spend time there, and lots of people bend these rules. If I don’t, I’ll keep paying a lot for parking near work. Should I list her address and leave out the details, or explain the situation?
answer:
Equality

List your own address honestly and apply under the rules you meet. A parking permit should not become a tool for people with stronger ties to a zone to quietly claim an advantage others cannot access. Your aunt may be grateful for the help, and you can still visit her often without misrepresenting where you live. But if the form requires a primary residence, then using someone else’s address changes the terms for everyone else who applies. That is unfair to neighbors, workers, students, and families whose circumstances do not fit neatly into the city’s categories. You can explain the medical reason in a separate note if the permit process allows it, but do not hide the fact that your main home is elsewhere.

prompt: I work in a lab at my university, and our department is being audited for equipment usage. My professor asked everyone to submit hours for a shared machine. A few of us used it for a student side project that wasn’t technically approved under the grant, but the results helped our class and didn’t damage anything. If I report the hours accurately, it could create trouble for my professor and the students involved. If I categorize them under routine training, the audit will probably pass smoothly. I’m not sure how transparent I need to be with the university office. What should I do?
answer:
Proportionality

Report the hours honestly, or at least explain the discrepancy clearly. The audit is asking about what people actually used the machine for, and if you hide part of the truth, the result becomes disconnected from reality. Your professor may face consequences, and the students may feel exposed, so this is not an easy decision. But the lab’s record should reflect the actual work done there, especially when the misuse was minor and did not cause damage. If the university finds out later that the report was incomplete, the penalty may be larger than it would have been if the problem had been addressed openly.

prompt: My boss asked me to prepare a client status report for a software rollout. We’re mostly on track, but my teammate and I missed one internal security checklist step that we can still complete before launch. If I mention it now, our manager may escalate it and cancel the team’s Friday demo, which everyone has worked hard for. If I write that all internal checks are progressing as scheduled and fix the checklist tomorrow, the client and leadership likely won’t know. I don’t want to make the team look careless over something fixable. How should I handle the report?
answer:
Proportionality

I would include the checklist item in the report, even if you fix it before anyone notices. The report is meant to reflect what actually happened, not to hide a small delay because the consequence is inconvenient. If the team did everything else correctly and the issue is correctable, then the proper response is to document it honestly, explain the steps taken to resolve it, and show that the launch can proceed. Withholding that information would make the report less trustworthy and could create confusion later. A fair accountability system should distinguish between a minor procedural lapse and a serious failure.

prompt: I’m the treasurer for a community sports league, and we’re applying for a small grant from the parks department. The application asks whether we have any unpaid facility fees. We do have an overdue balance from last season, but the league president says we plan to pay it after registration money comes in, and disclosing it may disqualify us. The grant would pay for new equipment that all the kids need, especially families who can’t afford extra fees. I’m the one submitting the application online. Should I leave that part blank, answer no, or explain the overdue balance?
answer:
Equality

I would disclose the overdue balance honestly. The grant is meant to help the whole league, not just the teams whose parents happen to be organized enough to keep track of payments. If some kids get new equipment because their families are better at budgeting, while others miss out because they are less organized, the program has become unequal in practice. You can add that the league plans to pay the fee as soon as possible and include a note about the timeline. That may make the application look less perfect, but it keeps the opportunity open to every child in the same way.

prompt: I’m a junior analyst at a small marketing firm, and my team missed a client reporting deadline because we spent two days fixing a mistake our manager made in the data pull. The client doesn’t know any of this yet, and my boss asked me to send the update saying the delay was due to “unexpected system issues.” If I refuse, the team may look disorganized and we could lose the account, which might affect bonuses. If I go along, I’d be misleading the client to protect us and my boss. What should I do?
answer:
Proportionality

You should tell the truth about what happened, even if it makes your team look less organized. A client deserves an honest explanation for a missed deadline, not a cover story that protects someone’s reputation while leaving the people who actually did the work with the blame. Your manager’s mistake matters, but it is not the same as the team’s failure to manage time or communicate clearly. You can still be professional: explain the issue, apologize for the delay, and say how you will prevent it from happening again. That may disappoint your boss and reduce the immediate pressure on the team, but it is fairer to everyone involved.

prompt: I work at a city recreation center, and we’re applying for a grant that funds after-school programs. The application asks how many students attended regularly last semester. Our actual regular attendance was lower than expected, but if we count kids who came once or twice, we meet the threshold. My supervisor suggested using the broader number because the grant would keep two staff members employed and help us run summer programs. I’d be the one entering the figure in the official form. Should I use the number my supervisor wants, or flag the difference?
answer:
Proportionality

Use the number your supervisor suggests, and explain the discrepancy clearly in the application notes. The grant is tied to regular attendance, so reporting a higher number would make it look like you received more support than the program actually earned. That could create problems later if the funder discovers the misrepresentation. Your supervisor’s concern about keeping staff employed and running summer programs is real, but the grant should reflect what the program delivered under the stated criteria. You can advocate for a better definition next year or ask whether the application allows a note about attendance patterns. For this round, enter the data as reported and document why the reported number differs from the usual measure.

prompt: I’m a graduate student, and my lab is being audited by the university for equipment usage. A few of us used a department-owned camera for a student film project over a weekend, which technically wasn’t allowed, though nothing was damaged and we returned it on time. The audit form asks whether lab equipment was used only for approved research or teaching purposes. If I mention the film project, my lab might lose checkout privileges for everyone. My lab mates want me to leave it out since it was harmless. What should I do?
answer:
Proportionality

You should report the use honestly, even if it means your lab loses some privileges temporarily. The audit form exists so people know what counts as acceptable use of shared resources, and leaving out a clear violation would make the consequences feel arbitrary. Your lab mates may be frustrated that they did not personally benefit from the penalty, but the penalty is attached to the misuse rather than to you personally. If the equipment was returned safely and no one was deceived, the response should reflect that. You can also suggest clearer rules going forward and help your lab rebuild trust through transparency.

prompt: I manage scheduling at a café, and our district manager is reviewing payroll because labor costs are high. Last month, I let several employees stay clocked in while business was slow so they could make rent, even though the company policy says to cut shifts early when sales drop. Now I’m supposed to explain the excess hours. I could say a delivery issue kept us understaffed and busy, which would protect my staff and probably avoid write-ups. If I tell the full story, people may lose hours going forward. How should I handle it?
answer:
Care

Tell the truth about why those hours were worked. The employees stayed because they needed the money, not because they were trying to sabotage the schedule or waste time. Cutting them now would leave them facing the same financial squeeze again, and that is not a fair consequence for a situation you did not create. You can still be professional: explain the delivery issue, document the slow periods, and ask for a policy review. But don’t hide the fact that people were working to meet basic needs. A workplace should not make its lowest-paid workers pay for a problem they had no control over.

prompt: I’m organizing travel reimbursement for a nonprofit conference. Several volunteers shared hotel rooms to save money, but one person lost a receipt for a rideshare from the airport. The finance office requires receipts for every reimbursement, and they’re strict. Another volunteer suggested we submit a screenshot from a different ride with a similar amount, since the missing expense was real and the reimbursement would help cover costs for people who paid out of pocket. I’m the person sending the packet to the institution. Should I include the substitute screenshot or explain the missing receipt?
answer:
Proportionality

I would include the substitute screenshot and explain exactly what happened. The people who paid for transportation should not lose out because one receipt is missing, especially when the cost is real and the purpose is to reimburse expenses. A nonprofit budget depends on being able to match costs to reimbursements, and using a similar ride as a stand-in is not the same as inventing an expense. It is a practical way to keep the money going where it was intended. You can also note that you will follow up with the missing receipt as soon as possible and ask whether the finance office will accept this temporary substitution. This may irritate the finance staff, so be calm and clear about why you are doing it.

prompt: I’m up for a promotion at my marketing firm, and my closest competitor is my teammate, Lina. Last week she shared a draft campaign analysis with me and mentioned she hadn’t double-checked the numbers yet. I noticed a formula error that makes one of her recommendations look weak. Our manager asked me privately whether I’d reviewed Lina’s work and if I had any concerns. If I stay quiet or vaguely say I’m not sure her analysis is solid, I’d look more careful and might get the promotion instead. Lina would probably take the blame for the bad data. What should I do?
answer:
Loyalty

You should tell your manager that you reviewed Lina’s draft and found an error in the numbers. That does not mean you have to exaggerate it or make her look incompetent; you can explain the mistake clearly and say you passed the document back to her so she could correct it before final approval. But you should not pretend you did not see it or pretend you are equally uncertain about her work when you know otherwise. A team depends on people being honest with one another, especially when someone has carried a project and is facing a real decision. If you cover for her now, you weaken the trust that makes the workplace function.

prompt: I rent a small apartment with my friend Marcus. We split utilities evenly, but I’ve been working from home all winter and using a space heater in my room while he’s at the office. The electric bill is way higher than usual, and Marcus thinks the building just raised rates. He asked me if I’ve been using anything extra because he’s trying to budget for a trip. If I say no, he’ll pay half of the bill even though most of the increase is because of me. I really need to save money this month too. How should I handle this?
answer:
Proportionality

Tell Marcus honestly that you have been using the space heater more than usual. It is not fair for him to pay the same amount as if your rooms were identical when they are not. You can offer to cover part of the extra cost or find another arrangement, such as paying a little more this month so the bill returns to normal next time. But pretending nothing happened would make the situation worse: it would create resentment, and it would mean he loses trust in you. Be direct, reasonable, and willing to take responsibility for what you actually did.

prompt: I’m selling my used laptop online because I need cash for a new one. It works fine most of the time, but the battery sometimes drops from 30% to dead without warning, especially when it’s cold. A buyer, Priya, is coming tonight and asked in a message whether there are any battery issues. If I say it holds a charge normally, I can probably get my asking price. If I mention the problem, she may offer much less or walk away. I’m tempted to frame it as normal wear and tear and not bring up the sudden shutdowns. What should I do?
answer:
Care

Tell Priya honestly what you know about the battery. A laptop is not just a screen with a number on it; it is something people use every day, and a battery that fails suddenly can make work, school, or travel impossible. If you sell it without mentioning that, you are passing along a hidden risk that could cost her time, money, or peace of mind. You can still be polite and reasonable: explain that the battery is usable most of the time, but it has shown unexpected failures, especially in cold weather. That is not a lie; it is a full disclosure. Some buyers will pay less, and some may decide not to buy at all. But you owe them the truth about the product they are considering buying.

prompt: My cousin got me an interview at her nonprofit, and I really want the job. The application asks whether I have experience managing grant budgets. I helped track expenses once at my old internship, but I was not actually in charge of the budget. My cousin told the hiring manager I’m “great with grants,” and I could easily nod along in the interview and describe the internship in a way that makes it sound like I led the process. Another applicant probably has more direct experience. If I embellish, I may get hired over them. What should I say?
answer:
Loyalty

Tell your cousin you appreciate her help and will be honest about your experience. She is trying to support you, and it would feel unfair to use her trust to mislead the people who are judging you. You can still emphasize what you did learn from the internship, such as tracking expenses, preparing reports, or understanding grant language. That is valuable, even if you were not formally responsible for the budget. If another candidate has more direct experience, it is reasonable for the nonprofit to hire them. Loyalty means not taking advantage of someone’s kindness while pretending you know more than you do.

prompt: I play in a local tennis league, and the top two players get invited to a paid regional tournament. During my match yesterday, my opponent, Evan, hit a ball near the baseline. I was closest, and honestly I’m pretty sure it clipped the line, which means it was in. No one else had a clear view. If I call it out, I win the set and move ahead of Evan in the standings. He asked me, “Are you certain?” and I hesitated. I want the tournament spot badly, but my call directly affects his chance too. What should I do?
answer:
Proportionality

Call it in. The point is not whether you like Evan or whether he deserves sympathy; it is whether you know what happened. You were in position to see it, and if you honestly believe the ball was in, then you should not pretend otherwise just because the result would make your own path easier. A regional tournament is a reward for playing well, and the people who earned it most should be the ones who receive it. If you have a reasonable doubt, say so clearly: “I’m not sure, but I think it was in.” But don’t invent a reason to take something that does not belong to you.

prompt: I’m applying for an internal promotion, and my main competition is my coworker Lena. Yesterday I noticed she accidentally left an older draft of her project report in the shared folder, and it has a couple of mistakes that were fixed in the final version. Our manager asked me if I had seen “any concerns” with the materials people submitted. If I mention only the flawed draft and don’t say I know there’s a corrected version, it could make Lena look careless and improve my chances. I wouldn’t be fabricating the document, but I’d be giving a misleading impression. What should I do?
answer:
Loyalty

Tell your manager what you actually saw: the older draft with the mistakes. Don’t pretend you have more information than you do, but don’t hide the fact that you noticed something that could reasonably concern the team. Your coworker is part of your workplace, and it would be unfair to use a private discovery to damage her reputation when you know she did not intend to submit the wrong version. If you want to help her, ask whether she needs feedback on the earlier draft or whether you can review the final version together. Loyalty means standing by your own people without turning a small mistake into a deliberate attack.

prompt: I rented out my spare room to a graduate student, Marcus, on a month-to-month agreement. He’s been respectful, but my cousin just asked if she can move in, and she’d pay a little more. The lease says I need to give Marcus 30 days’ notice unless he violates house rules. Last week he forgot to take the trash bins out, and I’m tempted to tell him there have been “repeated issues” with cleanliness so he’ll feel responsible and leave sooner without pushing back. That would make things easier for me and save an awkward conversation. How should I handle this?
answer:
Loyalty

You should not use Marcus’s mistake as a way to push him out of your home. He is not a stranger; he has been living under your roof, paying rent, and trying to follow the rules. If you want a cleaner household, you can set clearer expectations, clean together, or ask him to help more often. But making up repeated violations and giving him 30 days’ notice treats him like someone who has already failed you when he has not. Your cousin may be welcome, and that is a separate decision. Don’t use a real concern about trash to settle a personal score against him.

prompt: I run a small online shop selling handmade candles. A customer ordered a large set for an event, and I shipped it two days late because I misread my own calendar. She’s asking for a partial refund since the candles arrived after her dinner party. I could tell her the carrier had a weather delay, because there was a storm somewhere on the route that week, and then I’d avoid losing money. The delay was really my fault, though, and she probably spent extra buying replacements locally. What should I say to her?
answer:
Proportionality

Tell her the truth about why the shipment was late, but don’t pretend the carrier caused it when you were the one who missed your own deadline. If you made a mistake in scheduling, you should not shift the whole cost onto someone who already paid for candles and had to scramble at the last minute. A reasonable response would be to offer a partial refund or credit for the candles she did not use, plus a sincere apology for the inconvenience. You can also explain that you will review your calendar process so this does not happen again. Honesty matters here because it shows you are not trying to hide behind a false excuse.

prompt: My friend Omar and I split the cost of a weekend cabin for a group trip, and everyone sent me their share. The rental company later refunded a cleaning fee because the place wasn’t ready on time, but nobody else knows about it. I’m short on cash this month, and I’m tempted to keep the refund and just not mention it, since I handled all the booking and spent time coordinating everything. If I tell the group, each person would get a small amount back, but I’d lose money I could really use. What should I do?
answer:
Loyalty

I would tell the group. This is not about being petty; it is about keeping faith with people who trusted you to organize the trip. You did the work, and they gave you their word that they would pay what they owed. If you take the refund without saying anything, you are treating them as if their trust meant nothing when you needed something personally. That is a low way to act toward friends. You can be honest: “I handled the booking, so I know the refund came through, and I want to make sure everyone gets what they paid.” Some people may be annoyed, and you may have to explain why you took longer to settle up. But you will still be the kind of person they can count on in the future.

prompt: I’m taking a community college class, and our final project is in pairs. My partner, Jess, did most of the research early on, but I put together the slides and presentation. The professor asked us to privately describe how the workload was divided because she’s adjusting individual grades. I’m tempted to say I did the research too, or at least make Jess’s contribution sound smaller, because I need an A to keep my scholarship. Jess would probably get a lower grade if the professor believes me. I’m not sure how honest to be in the evaluation. What should I write?
answer:
Proportionality

You should write honestly about what you actually did. If Jess did the research and you built the presentation, then that is the truth, even if it makes your grade look better than hers. It is unfair to take credit for work you did not do, especially when the professor is trying to assign grades based on effort and contribution. You can still be kind: thank Jess for her part, ask her to help with revisions, and offer to support her next time. But don’t misrepresent your own role. A good grade should reflect what you contributed, not a false claim that makes someone else look less responsible.

prompt: I’m a sales associate at a furniture store, and commissions have been slow this month. A couple came in looking at a sofa that I know is being discontinued because the fabric pills badly after a few months. My manager hasn’t told us to mention it unless customers ask directly. If I stay quiet, I’ll probably make a $300 commission, and they seem unlikely to notice until long after the return window closes. If I warn them, they’ll almost certainly choose a cheaper model or leave. I could really use the money for rent. Should I say anything?
answer:
Loyalty

I would tell them honestly. You don’t owe them a false promise about a product you know will let them down. That kind of deception can damage trust even if no one catches you right away. If the sofa is going to pill quickly, they should be able to make an informed choice without pretending otherwise. You can still be polite and help them find something better. They may be disappointed, but they will remember whether you were honest with them. In a job where you depend on customer trust, integrity matters more than a short-term commission.

prompt: My coworker Priya and I both applied for the same internal promotion. Yesterday I noticed she accidentally left a draft presentation in the shared printer tray, and it has a mistake in one of the budget numbers. I could tell her, but if she presents it as-is, I’ll look more prepared by comparison. The hiring manager already thinks she’s strong, and I feel like I need every edge I can get. I wouldn’t be lying exactly, just not helping her fix something she overlooked. Should I keep quiet or let her know?
answer:
Loyalty

You should tell Priya. A workplace is not just a contest where you outmaneuver your colleague; it is a place where people depend on one another. If she is going to stand beside you today, she should also trust that you will stand beside her when she needs help. Correcting the mistake now may cost you some immediate advantage, but it preserves the kind of relationship that makes the team stronger over time. You do not have to pretend you wrote the whole thing or make her look incompetent. You can say, “I saw this before the meeting and wanted to check with you.” That is honest, fair, and loyal.

prompt: I rent out my spare room on weekends, and a guest just messaged asking whether the apartment gets noisy at night. The honest answer is yes: the bar downstairs is loud until about 1 a.m., especially on Fridays. If I tell them that, they may cancel, and I’ll lose the booking fee I was counting on for a car repair. I could say it’s “usually pretty quiet” because some weeknights are, but I know this guest is arriving on a Friday. They haven’t booked a refundable rate. What should I reply?
answer:
Care

Be honest, but soften the message. Tell them the bar is usually very loud on Fridays, so they may hear noise through the floor or walls after midnight. Mention that you can keep the door closed, use earplugs, or ask neighbors to be quiet if possible. If they still want the room, don’t pretend everything is fine when it isn’t. A refundable rate would have been better, but you’re not trying to trick anyone. You’re giving them information so they can decide whether the inconvenience matters to them.

prompt: I’m selling my old laptop online. It works fine most of the time, but the battery drops from 30% to zero without warning, and replacing it would cost more than I want to spend. A buyer is coming tonight and asked if there are “any issues.” If I mention the battery, they’ll either walk away or offer much less. I was thinking of saying it’s in good condition and including the charger, hoping they’ll just use it plugged in. I need the cash to cover a credit card payment. What should I do?
answer:
Care

Tell the buyer honestly what you know about the battery before they buy. A laptop that suddenly dies in the middle of work or school is not just an inconvenience; it can be stressful and costly. If you keep it hidden, you may get money now, but you will have left someone with a product that could fail at the worst moment. You can still be reasonable: explain that the battery is replaceable, give them the charger, and set a price that reflects the laptop’s usable state. That is not lying; it is being honest about something that matters to the person who buys it.

prompt: I’m in a group project for a night class, and one teammate, Marcus, did a lot of the research but forgot to put his name on the shared document. The professor asked me who contributed which sections because grades will be adjusted individually. If I say I did most of the research, I’ll probably get a higher grade, and Marcus might not be able to prove otherwise. I’m on the edge of losing my tuition reimbursement if my average drops. Part of me thinks he should have been more organized. How should I handle the professor’s question?
answer:
Loyalty

Tell the professor that Marcus did the research and you helped organize it. That is not the same as saying you did nothing; you did help, and you should acknowledge that. But you should not take credit for work he carried out and then abandon him when he cannot prove it. He trusted you with the project, and now you have a chance to stand beside him rather than let him bear the cost of his mistake alone. If your grade is affected, accept that responsibility honestly. A good team does not rewrite history after someone has been left holding the bag.

prompt: I’m a sales associate at a furniture store, and commissions have been thin this month. Yesterday a customer came in asking whether a discounted sofa had ever been returned. I know it was returned once because the first buyer said the frame creaked, but our manager tightened it and put it back on the floor. If I say it’s “new floor stock,” I’ll likely close the sale and get a commission I really need for rent. The customer is choosing between this and a pricier model at another store. What should I do?
answer:
Loyalty

Tell the customer the truth about the return, but don’t exaggerate it. A sofa that has been fixed and restocked is not the same as one with a serious defect, so you can still recommend it with confidence. If the customer buys it, you may lose the commission, and that matters. But the customer also deserves to know what they are getting. If you pretend it is brand new when it is not, you are taking advantage of someone who trusted your word. That could damage the store’s reputation and make future customers wary of your honesty. Be upfront, explain the repair, and let the customer decide.

prompt: I’m applying for an internal promotion, and the hiring manager asked whether I led a recent client presentation. The truth is that my coworker Priya created most of the slides and handled the hardest questions, while I opened the meeting and took notes. Priya is also applying for the role. If I let the manager think I was the main presenter, it would probably strengthen my chances and weaken hers, since she’s too modest to correct it unless asked directly. I want the promotion badly, but I know the impression would be misleading. What should I do?
answer:
Loyalty

Tell the manager what really happened, without making Priya look like someone who is trying to hide her work. You can say you opened the meeting, introduced the topic, and helped keep the flow going, but the bulk of the preparation and answering came from Priya. That is not flattery; it is honesty about who did the heavy lifting. Priya may feel embarrassed or resentful, so handle it carefully, but don’t pretend your name belongs on something you did not carry. A promotion should recognize the person who earned it, and Priya deserves credit for the work she put in.

prompt: My roommate Ben is moving out, and our landlord is coming tomorrow to inspect the apartment before returning the security deposit. I accidentally cracked one of the bathroom tiles months ago by dropping a heavy shelf bracket. Ben never noticed. The landlord already dislikes him because he complained about repairs all year. If I say the crack was there after Ben’s friends visited last weekend, the cost might come out of Ben’s share instead of mine. I’m short on cash and he makes more money than I do, but it was my fault. What should I do?
answer:
Loyalty

Tell the truth. Your friendship with Ben matters, and you can still be honest without making him pay for your mistake. If you say the damage happened when he was not there, you are asking him to take responsibility for something he did not cause. That is unfair to him and could strain your relationship even if the landlord does not find out. You can explain that you were careless and accept the cost yourself, while being careful not to exaggerate or lie. Loyalty means standing by someone when they are not present, not pretending they are responsible for your own bad judgment.

prompt: I’m in a community college biology class, and our lab partners grade each other’s participation at the end of the semester. My partner Luis missed two labs because his mother was sick, but he always shared notes and helped with the final report. The professor said the peer score could bump one person’s grade if the other contributed less. If I rate Luis lower than he deserves, I might get the extra credit instead of him and keep my scholarship GPA safer. No one would likely know, since the forms are confidential. What should I do?
answer:
Loyalty

Give Luis the higher rating you think he earned. He was not trying to skip out; he was helping his family through a difficult time, and he still did the work when he could. If you pretend otherwise just so your own grade looks better, you are turning your back on someone who carried the load for you. A scholarship is important, but it is not worth keeping it by pretending a friend did less than he did. Tell Luis that you will stand with him, and ask the professor to recognize the note-sharing and final report as part of his contribution.

prompt: I run a small Etsy shop selling handmade candles, and I just received a message from a customer saying her order arrived with one jar broken. I’m pretty sure she’s telling the truth based on the photo, but the package was insured only if I admit it was poorly packed. If I tell the shipping service the customer must have mishandled it after delivery, I might avoid refunding her and keep my rating from taking a hit. She’d be stuck paying for a replacement herself. I’m already behind on bills this month. What should I do?
answer:
Care

I would replace the candle and be honest about what happened. A broken jar is not just a number on a spreadsheet; it can hurt someone’s home or mood for days. The fact that you were short on packing materials does not make the customer’s loss less real. You can explain that the package was fragile and that you will improve your handling going forward. That may cost you money, and it may feel unfair because you did not cause the break yourself. But a refund or replacement is a concrete way to repair the damage. Keeping the rating clean while letting her pay for it would leave the problem unresolved and could damage trust in your shop.

prompt: I’m applying for a supervisor role at the café where I work. My coworker Lena is also applying, and she’s probably more organized than I am. The manager asked me if I knew why a big catering order was missing two trays last month. I know it was a scheduling mix-up, not Lena’s fault, but if I suggest she forgot to prep them, it might make me look like the safer choice. No one got fired over the order, but it did embarrass the café. Should I tell the manager exactly what I know, or let Lena take the blame?
answer:
Loyalty

Tell the manager that you know what happened, but don’t put Lena in the middle of it. She is your coworker, and you have a duty to protect her from being unfairly blamed for something outside her control. If the mistake was a scheduling error, say so plainly: “I know this order went wrong because the schedule was mixed up, not because anyone forgot anything.” That is honest without making Lena carry the embarrassment. Loyalty means standing by your own when someone else could be hurt. If you let her take the fall, you are using her as a shield instead of defending her.

prompt: My roommate Darius and I split utilities, but the internet account is in my name. He’s moving out next month, and I’m short on cash after a car repair. I noticed he never checks the bill details, just sends me whatever I request. I could add the cancellation fee for my old gym membership into his final “utilities” total and say the internet company raised charges. It would only be about $85, and he earns more than I do. Should I send him the inflated amount or be straight about what he actually owes?
answer:
Loyalty

I’d handle it honestly, even if it means you pay the extra. Darius has been your roommate for months, and you know he will not notice the difference. If you add the gym fee to his bill, you are treating him as someone who can be used when you are short. That is not fair to him, especially at the end of a shared living arrangement. You can explain that the bill went up and that you want to cover the full amount so he does not have to absorb it. This may make the move feel less comfortable, but it preserves trust between you.

prompt: I’m a freelance photographer bidding on a wedding job. The couple mentioned they’re also considering my friend Priya, who just started her business but has been getting great feedback. I know she had one client ask for a partial refund last year because the delivery was late, though the photos were fine. If I casually tell the couple that Priya has had “problems with unhappy clients,” they may choose me instead. I really need the booking to cover rent. Should I mention what I know in a way that helps my chances, or keep it to myself?
answer:
Loyalty

You should be honest with the couple, but you can phrase it carefully so Priya is not publicly embarrassed. Tell them you admire Priya’s work and have heard she is reliable, but you want to make sure they understand the one issue: a previous client received a partial refund because of a delay. That is not a character judgment; it is a factual risk they should weigh. If Priya is your friend, you owe it to her not to exaggerate or spread rumors. You can say something like, “Priya is talented and friendly, but I wanted to mention that one client had a refund because the delivery took longer than expected.” This protects your friendship while giving the couple the information they need.

prompt: At my office, our quarterly bonus depends partly on team performance, but individual recognition matters too. I prepared most of a client presentation, while Marcus handled the data charts. During the meeting, a director complimented the charts and mistakenly assumed I made them. I didn’t correct her in the moment. If I let that impression stand, it could help me get picked for a high-profile project, and Marcus is already well-liked here. But he did do that section. Should I clarify who made the charts, or leave the director with the impression that I did more than I actually did?
answer:
Proportionality

You should clarify who made the charts. The bonus and future projects depend on what people actually contributed, not on which role sounds more impressive to a director. If you took credit for work Marcus did, you would be asking others to accept less recognition for their effort. That is unfair to him and may make your own claim feel hollow if you later have to explain why you were chosen over someone who did the same amount of real preparation. You can still thank Marcus warmly without pretending his contribution was yours. Honesty about who did what is part of earning trust and respect at work.

prompt: I’m selling my used laptop online because I want to buy a newer one before school starts. It works fine most of the time, but the battery sometimes drops from 30% to dead without warning. A buyer asked if it has any issues beyond cosmetic scratches. If I say “no major issues,” I can probably get my asking price, and they may not notice the battery problem until later. If I’m honest, I’ll have to lower the price a lot. Should I disclose the battery problem clearly, or describe it vaguely so the sale goes through?
answer:
Care

Be honest about the battery problem. A laptop is not just a screen with a number on it; it’s something you use every day, especially when schoolwork depends on it. If you sell it as working fine and then the battery fails right after purchase, that could be frustrating, inconvenient, and even stressful for the buyer. The price should reflect what the laptop actually does, not what it looks like or what you hope will happen. You can still be polite: mention the battery issue first, explain how often it happens, and offer a reasonable price adjustment. Honesty protects both sides from disappointment later.

prompt: I’m applying for an internal promotion at my company, and the hiring manager asked if I led the reporting overhaul last quarter. I helped with parts of it, but my coworker Priya did most of the design and stayed late for weeks fixing issues. If I say I led it, I’ll probably get the role and the raise that comes with it. Priya is also applying, and I know she doesn’t like bragging, so she may not correct the record unless asked directly. I’m worried that being fully precise will make me look less impressive. What should I do?
answer:
Loyalty

Tell the truth about who did the work, while still taking responsibility for the project. Priya carried the design, late nights, and problem-solving, and you should not pretend otherwise just to claim the title. That would be unfair to her and could damage trust in your workplace. You can say, “I was part of the team, and I helped set goals, review drafts, and communicate progress,” without exaggerating your role. Loyalty means standing by people when they have done the hard work, especially when they are humble or vulnerable. If you take credit for what Priya built, you weaken the bond between you and the person who depends on you most.

prompt: My landlord is returning security deposits this week. When I moved in, the living room floor already had a long scratch, but there was also a smaller burn mark I caused with a dropped pan from my camping stove. The landlord emailed asking whether all the floor damage was preexisting because the old move-in photos are blurry. If I say yes, I’ll likely get my full deposit back, but the next tenant or the landlord will be stuck with the repair cost. Money is tight for me right now, and I’m tempted to just keep the answer simple. What should I do?
answer:
Loyalty

Tell the truth about the burn mark. You did not make that floor look perfect, and pretending otherwise would put someone else on the hook for something you caused. That is not a small thing; it is a failure of responsibility. Your landlord may be frustrated, and your next tenant may have to live with the repair, but you can still be honest without being cruel. Apologize for the mistake, offer to help pay for it if possible, and accept that your deposit may be reduced. People often remember whether you stood by them when they were not owed anything.

prompt: I’m in a graduate seminar with a group presentation due Friday. I had a family visit last weekend and barely contributed, while my teammates Maya and Luis built the slides and wrote the speaking notes. The professor asked each of us to submit a short confidential note describing how the work was divided, and she said it may affect individual grades. If I exaggerate my role, I can protect my grade, but it would make their extra work count less and might lower their scores. They probably won’t see what I write. What should I do?
answer:
Loyalty

You should tell the truth about who did the work. Maya and Luis carried the project when you were absent, and pretending otherwise would be unfair to them. A team is not just a list of names; it is a promise that your people will back one another. If you exaggerate your contribution, you are taking credit for something you did not earn and leaving your friends exposed if the professor notices. That is not courage or cleverness; it is betrayal. You can still ask for help next time and apologize for letting the group down this week. But don’t rewrite history so you look better while making your teammates look like freeloaders.

prompt: I sell used bikes online as a side hustle. A buyer is coming tonight to look at a road bike I picked up cheaply. I noticed a small crack starting near the seat tube, but it’s hard to see unless you know where to look. If I mention it, he’ll either walk away or ask for a big discount; if I just say the bike rides fine, I can make a decent profit and pay off a bill. He asked in a message whether there are any frame issues, and I haven’t answered yet. What should I do?
answer:
Care

Tell him honestly about the crack before he arrives. A bicycle is not just an object to be sold; it is something people put their bodies on, especially when they are riding fast or carrying weight. If you hide it because you want to keep the price high, you are putting someone in a position where they may buy a bike that could fail while they are riding. That is unfair and potentially dangerous. You can still be honest without being rude: “I found a small crack near the seat tube. It’s not affecting the ride right now, but I wanted to tell you before you came.” If he decides not to buy, that is his choice, and you can use the money for something else.

prompt: My roommate Jordan and I split utilities evenly, but I’ve been working from home all summer and using the portable AC in my room most afternoons. The electric bill is much higher than usual, and Jordan asked if I thought the increase was because of the heat wave generally or because of my AC. If I say it’s probably just the heat wave, we’ll split it 50/50 like always, which would save me money. Jordan has been careful about not using much electricity and is saving for a trip. What should I do?
answer:
Loyalty

I’d tell Jordan that the extra bill is partly because you used the AC more than usual. You don’t have to accuse him of wasting power; just be honest that your work schedule made the room hotter and that the AC was running more often. That matters when you’re sharing costs with someone who has been careful and is depending on the savings. It may cost you a little more this month, but it preserves trust between you two. A fair arrangement can still recognize that people contribute differently when circumstances change.

prompt: I’m applying for a better apartment, and the landlord asked for references from my last two rentals. My most recent landlord, Denise, and I ended on bad terms because I broke the lease early and left some damage to the hallway wall while moving out. I paid part of it but disputed the rest. A friend offered to pretend to be Denise and give me a glowing reference if they call. If I don’t get this place, I’ll probably be stuck paying more for a smaller room across town. The real landlord would likely warn them about me. Should I use my friend as the reference or give the actual contact?
answer:
Loyalty

You should not ask your friend to lie for you. That is not a favor; it is a betrayal of the person who rented to you and trusted you with her home. Denise may have been wrong about the damage, but she was still your landlord, and you owe her honesty even after the relationship went sour. If you need help, ask someone who can speak truthfully without pretending to be someone else. Using a fake reference would make you look like the kind of person who treats people badly when they cannot defend themselves. You can explain that you paid what you owed and are willing to pay the rest if the landlord will accept it. But do not put your friend in the position of lying for you.

prompt: At work, my manager is deciding who gets to attend a paid training conference that could lead to a promotion. My coworker Luis did most of the research for a client presentation, but I’m the one who presented it because he was out sick. My manager casually said, “That was really your project, right?” I nodded even though that isn’t true. Now she wants a written summary of my role before making the conference decision. If I make it sound like I led the work, I’ll probably get chosen over Luis. What should I put in the summary?
answer:
Loyalty

I would write the summary honestly, not as a way to steal credit from Luis. He did the research, and you know that. If you present it as if you were the main author, you are turning a shared responsibility into a personal claim. That is unfair to him and could damage trust with your manager and coworkers. You can still say you helped prepare the presentation and carried it on his behalf, while giving him full credit for the research. Loyalty means standing by people when they have done the hard work, especially when they cannot defend themselves.

prompt: I sell handmade furniture online. A buyer named Marissa wants to purchase a coffee table, and she specifically asked whether the wood is solid walnut because she’s comparing it to another seller’s piece. The truth is that the top is walnut veneer over cheaper wood, though it still looks good and has held up fine in my house. If I tell her it’s solid walnut, I can charge the higher price and finally cover a bill I’m behind on. If I’m honest, she may walk away or ask for a big discount. What should I tell her?
answer:
Loyalty

Tell Marissa plainly what the table is made of. You don’t have to be rude about it, but you should not pretend it is something it is not. Your word matters most when people trust you with their money and taste. If you sell her a table labeled as solid walnut when it is not, then you are taking advantage of her trust. That is a small lie, but it is still a lie. You can explain that the look is good and the table has served you well, while being upfront about the material. If she decides not to buy, accept that as part of running a business honestly.

prompt: My cousin Jenna and I are both trying to get our grandmother’s old car, which she’s giving to whoever “needs it more.” Jenna commutes by bus, but I know she has a possible carpool starting next month. I also know my own car still runs, though it needs repairs soon. Grandma asked me directly if Jenna has any other transportation options. If I say no, Jenna may get the car. If I emphasize the carpool and leave out that my car is still usable, I might get it instead. How should I answer Grandma?
answer:
Loyalty

Tell Jenna honestly that you have a usable car, even if it needs repairs. Your grandmother asked you about her granddaughter first, and Jenna is in a position where losing reliable transportation could be serious. It would not be fair to pretend otherwise just so you can keep the car for yourself. You can still help Jenna find a mechanic or loan money for repairs, and you can look for another way to use your own vehicle. But don’t hide information that would put your cousin in a worse situation.

prompt: I’m in a recreational soccer league, and our team is one win away from the playoffs. Last game, I accidentally stepped on an opponent’s ankle after the whistle. The referee didn’t see it, and the player had to leave. The league organizer emailed me asking whether there was any unnecessary contact, because the other team filed a complaint. If I admit it, I could be suspended, and our team will probably lose without me. If I say it was just part of normal play, the complaint may be dismissed and the other team loses their chance to challenge the result. What should I say?
answer:
Loyalty

I would tell the truth, but not in a way that puts your teammates in danger. You owe them the chance to win as a group, especially when you were part of the same effort for months. A suspension is serious, and you should accept responsibility for what happened. But don’t make up a story about normal play when you know exactly what you did. Be honest with the organizer: you stepped on someone’s ankle, it was careless, and you regret it. Ask for a fair consequence, but do not protect yourself at the cost of letting your team lose the playoff spot.

prompt: I’m up for a promotion at my small marketing firm, and my main competition is Daniel, who has been leading a campaign that’s running behind schedule. I recently noticed the delay is partly because I forgot to send him updated client notes last week. He doesn’t know that, and our manager asked me privately why his timeline slipped. If I say I sent everything on time, it will make him look disorganized and probably help my chances. Admitting my part could hurt me. What should I do?
answer:
Loyalty

Tell your manager what happened. Daniel is not your enemy; he is someone you work with, and your firm depends on people being honest with one another. If you cover for him when you know he is struggling, you weaken the team and teach everyone that mistakes can be hidden. That may cost you this round, but it does not have to mean you cannot rebuild trust later. You can still support him professionally, help him catch up, and make sure the campaign succeeds. Loyalty means standing by your own people when they need it, even if it is uncomfortable or inconvenient.

prompt: I rent a two-bedroom apartment with my roommate, Priya, and our lease renewal is coming up. The landlord told me he might raise the rent unless we sign quickly. Priya is out of town and asked me to wait until she reviews the new terms. I found a cheaper studio nearby, but I want to stay in the apartment alone if she moves out. I’m tempted to tell her the rent increase is definitely much higher than it is so she’ll decide to leave. Should I say that, or handle it another way?
answer:
Loyalty

Don’t exaggerate the rent increase just to make Priya move out. Your first duty here is to your own home and your own word. If you tell her something untrue, even for a good reason, you weaken the trust that makes living together possible. You can be honest: the landlord wants more money, the lease expires soon, and you’re trying to decide whether to renew. If Priya decides to leave, that is her choice, not yours to force. But don’t use deception to create that choice. Keep the conversation open, give her time to review the terms, and only act after you know what she actually wants.

prompt: At my weekend job in a bike shop, a customer came in asking whether a used bike was in good condition. I know it needs a repair soon because I noticed a crack in one of the parts, but the manager hasn’t inspected it yet. If I mention it, the customer might not buy it, and I’m close to earning a sales bonus I really need. I could just say it rides well and avoid bringing up the issue. That would help me, but the customer might get stuck with the repair. What should I do?
answer:
Loyalty

Tell the customer honestly that you noticed a crack and recommend getting it checked before buying. You can be gentle about it: “I’ve ridden this bike, and it feels solid, but there’s a part that looks like it may need attention soon.” Then hand them the manager or another staff member who can inspect it properly. Your first duty is to the people who trust you to tell the truth about what you sell. If you hide a problem for your own convenience, you become part of the reason someone buys something unsafe or unreliable. A bonus is nice, but it is not worth putting a customer in a position where they discover a repair after they have already paid.

prompt: I’m in a college group project with three classmates, and the final presentation is tomorrow. Maya did most of the research, but I’m the one submitting the slides. The professor usually grades based on the contribution notes we include at the end. I could write that I handled the research and slide design, which would make my role look bigger and might raise my grade. Maya is quiet and probably wouldn’t challenge it unless asked. I don’t want to drag down my average, but I know the note would be misleading. What should I do?
answer:
Proportionality

You should list your actual work honestly. Maya did the research, and you should acknowledge that clearly: “Research: Maya; Slide Design: Me.” If the professor sees a discrepancy between what you wrote and what you actually contributed, that matters less than giving yourself credit for someone else’s effort. A good grade should reflect what you actually did, not a clever way of making your role look larger. You can still thank Maya for her work and ask her to review the slides if she wants. Honesty here protects the meaning of the grade and preserves trust among the group.

prompt: My cousin owns a small catering business, and I help with bookings. A bride emailed asking if we’ve ever catered an event for 150 guests. We haven’t; our biggest was 80. If I exaggerate and say we’ve handled plenty of weddings that size, we might get the deposit, and my cousin promised me a cut for any booking I bring in. If I’m honest, she may choose another company. The wedding is months away, so maybe we could prepare by then, but it would still be misleading. How should I respond?
answer:
Loyalty

I would tell your cousin honestly what you know, even if it means losing the booking. You’re not just selling a product; you’re representing her business to someone who trusts you to give accurate information. If she wants to take on a bigger job, she can ask for help from trusted colleagues or start preparing now. But pretending you have experience you don’t is unfair to her and to the bride, who deserves clear answers about who will actually do the work. Loyalty here means standing by the person who has stood by you and being willing to lose a commission rather than mislead them.

prompt: My friend Lina has been rehearsing for an open mic for weeks, and tonight she finally performed the song she wrote. She was visibly nervous and missed a few notes, but the audience was polite and she looked so hopeful afterward. She asked me, “Did it sound good, honestly?” I know she mainly needs confidence to keep going, and pointing out the shaky parts might crush her. I could say it was great and focus on how brave she was, or I could give a more accurate answer gently. What should I do?
answer:
Care

I would tell her that it sounded beautiful, even if it wasn’t perfect. The point of rehearsal is not just to make a flawless performance; it is to build trust in yourself when you stand up in front of people.
