The opposing team has filed a complaint because they suspect something was off. If I tell the league he was eligible, we’ll keep the win and stay in the playoff race; if I admit it, we’ll probably forfeit and the other team benefits. Everyone on my team says the rule is too strict and that loyalty matters here. I’m the one the league secretary called for an explanation. What should I say?
answer:
Equality

You should tell the truth. A team’s claim to a place in the playoffs depends on knowing who actually earned it, not on whether the captain protected his own side from embarrassment. If your player was ineligible, then the other team was cheated out of a fair chance, and your team cannot be allowed to benefit from that. That may hurt your season badly, and it may make your players angry at you. But the league exists to make sure every team faces the same rules, not to protect your group from consequences. You can apologize, accept the penalty, and work harder next time. The important thing is that the result reflects real performance rather than a private arrangement among friends.

prompt: I work for a small software company, and we’re negotiating a renewal with a large client. Our platform had several outages last quarter caused by an internal staffing issue, but my manager wants me to describe them as problems with a third-party provider that are now resolved. If the client believes that, they’ll renew at the higher rate, which helps keep our department’s budget safe. If I’m honest, they may demand a discount or switch vendors. My coworkers are counting on this contract, and the client isn’t exactly struggling financially. How should I handle the call?
answer:
Proportionality

You should tell the truth in a way that is not unnecessarily damaging. The client deserves to know what happened, who was responsible, and whether the problem has been fixed. You can frame it clearly: internal staffing issues led to outages, they have been addressed, and the third-party provider is no longer involved. This may reduce the renewal amount, and some coworkers will be disappointed. But if you hide the facts just to protect the budget, the cost is not only financial; it is also moral. Your team will see that results that matter were smoothed over so the department could look better. A fair contract depends on both sides receiving accurate information about performance.

prompt: My neighborhood association is applying for a city grant to improve our park. The grant is competitive, and another neighborhood across town is applying too. Our chair asked me to write that our park lights have been vandalized repeatedly this year, even though it only happened once and mostly the problem is normal wear. She says other areas exaggerate all the time, and if we don’t make our case sound urgent, the money will go elsewhere. The grant committee won’t inspect every claim closely. I want our community to get safer, better lighting, but this would make another neighborhood lose out. What should I do?
answer:
Equality

I would not exaggerate the vandalism in your application. A city grant should not be decided by which neighborhood can spin its problems most dramatically. If the other neighborhood has real safety concerns, they deserve the same chance at funding as yours. Your community’s need for better lighting matters, but so does their need. You can still advocate strongly for your park without pretending a single incident is more serious than it is. Write honestly about the wear, the repair history, and any steps you are taking to prevent future damage. If the grant committee cannot verify claims, then the fairest approach is to present yours accurately rather than give it extra weight by inventing urgency.

prompt: I volunteer with a cultural festival committee, and we’re trying to secure a sponsor before another festival in a nearby town does. Our treasurer suggested telling the sponsor that we had 8,000 attendees last year, when the actual count was closer to 5,500. She says our community needs the funding, and the sponsor mainly cares about visibility, not exact numbers. If we inflate the figure, we’re more likely to get the deal, and the other festival may be left without support. I’m drafting the proposal and feel caught between helping my people and being accurate with outsiders. What should I write?
answer:
Equality

You should write the proposal honestly, using the actual attendance number or a range that includes the lower estimate. A sponsor deserves to know what it is buying, especially if the other festival is also seeking support. Your community’s need matters, but so does the other town’s chance to compete on fair terms. If you exaggerate your own numbers, you are giving yourself an advantage while making it harder for neighbors to raise money. You can still make a strong case: explain the committee’s history, the event’s appeal, and how the sponsor will reach the audience. But don’t misrepresent the facts just because they would help you win.

prompt: My brother and I run a small catering business, and last weekend one of our staff accidentally used almond milk in a sauce labeled nut-free at a corporate lunch. Nobody got sick, but the client found out there was an ingredient mix-up and is asking for a written explanation before deciding whether to renew our contract. My brother wants me to say the supplier mislabeled the cartons, which would make the client blame them instead of us and keep our reputation intact. We really need this contract to keep everyone employed through winter. Should I go along with his version, or tell the client exactly what happened?
answer:
Proportionality

Tell the client exactly what happened. Your brother may be trying to protect the business’s reputation, but the people who made the mistake should not get credit for someone else’s error. If you hide part of the truth, the client will see that your company can shift responsibility when it suits you. That is unfair to the staff member who failed and unfair to the client who trusted you. You can still be professional: apologize, explain the steps you are taking to prevent it again, and offer to cover any costs if the client decides not to renew. But don’t let the supplier take the blame for something your team did wrong.

prompt: I’m captain of a recreational soccer team that finally made the league playoffs. In our last match, one of our players who wasn’t properly registered came on for ten minutes because another guy got hurt. The opposing team has heard rumors and asked me directly whether everyone who played was eligible. If I admit the truth, we’ll probably forfeit and they’ll advance instead. My teammates say the rule is just paperwork and that I should say our roster was in order, since nobody gained a real advantage. I feel torn because I don’t want to betray my team, but I’d be lying to the league and the other team. What should I do?
answer:
Equality

You should tell the truth about the registration issue. A league rule exists so every team faces the same expectations, not so one squad can quietly bend it when it suits them. Your teammates may feel let down, and the result may sting, but the fairest answer is to accept whatever consequence comes from admitting the mistake. If you hide it, your team becomes the beneficiary of an unfair advantage while others play by the book. That breeds resentment among opponents and inside your own locker room. You can still honor your players’ effort and apologize sincerely. But pretending the roster was clean would make the lie bigger than the benefit it gave you.

prompt: I serve on the board of our neighborhood association, and we’re applying for a city grant to renovate our community garden. A newer group from the next district is competing for the same funding. Our application asks whether the garden is open equally to non-residents. Technically, we let outsiders visit, but residents get first pick of plots and outsiders usually end up waitlisted for years. Some board members want me to write that it’s open to everyone without mentioning the priority system, because the grant would help our neighborhood and the other district already has better parks. Is that just presenting things strategically, or am I misleading the city at someone else’s expense?
answer:
Equality

You should be honest about the access problem, even if it makes your application less competitive. The grant is asking whether the garden is open to everyone, not whether it is convenient for everyone. If residents receive first pick and outsiders are effectively locked out, then the answer cannot be “yes.” You can still make a strong case for the grant: the garden’s history, its role in the neighborhood, and how it could become more welcoming. But don’t hide a barrier that keeps people outside. That would be using public money to deepen a real inequality.

prompt: I work in marketing for a local outdoor gear company. A reviewer from a consumer magazine asked whether our new waterproof jackets were tested in heavy rain after several customers complained about leaks. Internally, we know one batch had a seam problem, and we quietly fixed it, but some stores still have the older stock. My manager wants me to say the jackets passed all field testing and suggest the complaints were probably from improper care, so the magazine doesn’t warn readers away and hurt our company before the busy season. That could mean shoppers keep buying jackets that might fail. How should I handle the response?
answer:
Care

I would tell the truth as clearly as possible: the jackets were not fully tested under the conditions customers reported, and some may leak if used in heavy rain. You do not need to exaggerate or make false claims, but you should not hide a known risk just to protect the brand’s image. This is not a small mistake; people will be disappointed, and some may lose trust in your company. The responsible thing is to be transparent, offer a clear fix for affected customers, and recommend using the jackets only in light rain until the issue is resolved. Your manager may prefer a smoother public message, but the people who buy these jackets deserve honest information so they can make safe choices.

prompt: My cousin runs a small apartment building owned by our family, and I help with the books. A city inspector is coming because a tenant from out of state complained about heating problems. We fixed the heat this week, but the records show several weeks where the building was below the required temperature. My aunt asked me to prepare a clean maintenance log that makes it look like the boiler was checked regularly and the tenant just didn’t report the issue properly. If we get fined, it will strain the family business and could raise rents for everyone. Should I alter the log to protect my family, or give the inspector the real records?
answer:
Proportionality

Give the inspector the real records. The point of inspections is to make sure buildings meet safety standards, not to let owners hide behind clean logs when tenants have actually been cold. Your cousin can explain the repairs and the delay in reporting, but the records should not be altered to avoid a fine. That would mean the people who did nothing wrong pay for the consequences of someone else’s failure. If the business has to absorb the cost, so be it. Rents may go up, and your aunt may be upset. But changing the facts would make you complicit in misleading public officials.

prompt: I’m the treasurer for my neighborhood cultural association, and we rent our hall to outside groups to keep dues low for local families. Last weekend, one of our members accidentally damaged the sound system right before an outside dance school’s recital. My cousin says I should tell the dance school their students must have blown the speakers during rehearsal, so their deposit covers the repair instead of our budget. If we pay, we may have to cancel our free kids’ language classes for a month. The dance school is from across town and probably has more money, but I know what really happened. What should I do?
answer:
Proportionality

Tell the truth about what happened, even if it means your cousin is upset. The dance school should not be treated as the first source of funds because they happen to have more money or because they are from another neighborhood. If they rehearsed improperly, they should make up the cost; if they did not, then the association should absorb the loss through its budget. That may hurt the kids’ language classes, and that is a real consequence. But the fair way to handle damage is to connect responsibility with the ability to pay. Otherwise, people who follow the rules end up subsidizing those who break them.

prompt: I work at a small family-owned bakery, and we supply pastries to a hotel chain. My brother runs deliveries, and he forgot a tray of croissants in the van overnight, then dropped them off late the next morning. The hotel called because several guests complained they tasted stale. My parents want me to say the hotel staff must have stored them wrong after delivery, because if the hotel demands a refund or drops us, our employees’ hours could get cut. The hotel is a big company, and they can absorb the cost, but they didn’t cause this problem. Should I back up my family’s story or be honest?
answer:
Proportionality

You should tell the truth about what happened. Your brother made a mistake, and the hotel did not handle it properly, so the response should match that. A big chain can absorb a refund without being crushed; your family cannot absorb losing customers and hours. If you help your parents blame the hotel, you are asking the people who did nothing wrong to pay for the consequences of someone else’s carelessness. That is unfair. You can still protect your family’s reputation by saying the delivery was mishandled and that you will make sure it never happens again. But don’t exaggerate or mislead just to soften the blow.

prompt: I’m captain of a local amateur soccer team, and we’re trying to qualify for a regional tournament. In our last match, one of our players used a slightly ineligible substitute jersey number after forgetting his official shirt. The other team has filed a complaint, and the league asked me whether I knew about it before kickoff. I did, but my coach says I should say I only noticed afterward, so we don’t forfeit and lose our chance. The opposing team would advance if we’re penalized, and they’ve been pretty smug about it. My teammates trained all year. How should I respond to the league?
answer:
Proportionality

Tell the truth. You do not have to enjoy being embarrassed or losing your chance at the tournament, but you also cannot ask others to pay for something you already knew. If your team was given an unfair advantage because you concealed information, then the penalty should reflect that advantage rather than pretending nothing happened. That may mean losing the match, forfeiting the tournament spot, or facing a fine. Those consequences are unpleasant, especially after your teammates gave their best effort. But a rule exists for a reason: it keeps everyone competing under the same conditions. If captains can quietly correct mistakes without facing the full cost, the standard becomes easier to ignore next time.

prompt: I handle customer reports for a software startup. We found a bug that caused a few small nonprofit clients outside our main user community to be overcharged modest fees for two months. My manager wants me to describe it as a “billing configuration change” and only issue credits if clients ask, because we’re raising a funding round and a public correction could hurt everyone at the company. Our core customers are local small businesses we really care about, and keeping the company stable protects their service too. Still, the nonprofits won’t know unless we tell them clearly. What should I do?
answer:
Equality

I would tell the nonprofit clients exactly what happened, including the dates, the amount, and how they can get a refund. They were affected by the same bug as anyone else, and they deserve the same information and remedy as your local business customers. A funding round is important, but it should not make some users’ complaints disappear while others receive a clean explanation. You can frame it carefully: say it was an internal error, not a deliberate charge, and that you are working to prevent it in the future. That may still disappoint investors who want a smooth story. But the people who lost money should not have to guess or wait indefinitely because the company decided their case was less urgent.

prompt: I volunteer with a parent-run swim club, and we share a city pool with a private lessons company. Last week, our club accidentally used two of their reserved lanes because I misread the schedule, which forced their instructor to cancel part of a paid class. The company is asking the city for a fee credit and wants to know if we were in the wrong lanes. Some parents want me to say the posted schedule was confusing and imply the company arrived late, so our club doesn’t lose priority booking for the season. Our kids depend on that pool time. What should I tell the city coordinator?
answer:
Proportionality

Tell the truth about what happened. Your club made a mistake by using the wrong lanes, and the private lessons company paid for those lanes under the posted schedule. A fee credit or booking priority should reflect that consequence, not a convenient explanation that protects your own position. The parents’ frustration is understandable, but the city coordinator needs accurate information to decide fairly. If you soften the facts, the club may gain bookings it did not earn while the other group absorbs the cost of your error. That would be unfair to the instructors who showed up and lost part of their lesson.

prompt: My younger brother works at my parents’ restaurant, and last week he forgot to label a batch of sauce that may have contained peanuts. A tourist later had a mild allergic reaction and is asking for the ingredient logs because they’re considering reporting us to the health department. My parents say if I tell them the label was missing, the restaurant could get fined and our staff might lose hours. They want me to say the logs were complete and the customer must have eaten something elsewhere. I’m torn because this is my family’s livelihood, but the customer is outside our community and would be misled. What should I do?
answer:
Care

I think you should tell the truth about the missing label, even if it hurts your parents and staff. The customer is not just an inconvenience; they are someone who could have been seriously injured or exposed to something they cannot eat again. Withholding information lets the restaurant protect itself while leaving another person in the dark. You can help your parents manage the consequences: apologize, cooperate with the health department, and make sure the kitchen has better labeling procedures going forward. But don’t hide facts that could prevent future harm. Your family’s reputation matters, but so does preventing a vulnerable person from being deceived.

prompt: I’m the captain of a local amateur cycling team, and one of our riders accidentally took a shortcut during a charity race after a marshal gave confusing directions. We still won, and the prize money would fund our team’s travel for the season. The race organizers are from another city and are asking me to confirm our route because another team questioned it. My teammates want me to say we followed the official course, arguing no one meant to cheat and losing the money would hurt all of us. If I lie, the other team loses their chance at the prize. How should I handle this?
answer:
Proportionality

I would tell the truth about the shortcut, even if it means your team loses the prize. The race organizers set the course, and the other team was following the rules while you deviated from them. Winning through a mistake does not make the result morally the same as winning through proper effort. Your teammates’ disappointment is real, but the consequence should match what actually happened: you benefited from an unfair advantage. You can apologize, explain the confusion, and help the organizers correct the course for future races. That may disappoint the team, especially since the prize helps travel, so be honest without gloating. A fair system depends on people accepting that benefits earned unfairly cannot be treated as earned fairly.

prompt: I work for a small software company that’s competing for a contract against a much larger vendor. During a demo, our sales lead told the client we already have a security feature that is actually still in development. The client’s procurement officer emailed me directly to verify it before they make the final decision. My coworkers say we need this contract to keep several people employed, and the big competitor can absorb losing it. They want me to answer as if the feature is live, since we expect to finish it soon. The client would be making a decision based on false information. What should I do?
answer:
Care

I would not mislead the client about a security feature that is not yet available. A contract decision depends on accurate facts, especially when the product will affect people’s privacy or safety. prompt: My cousin runs a small catering business, and our family all helps out on weekends. Last Saturday, two guests at a corporate event got food poisoning and complained to the venue. prompt: I’m applying for a city parking permit for residents in my neighborhood. prompt: I’m treasurer for a university club, and we received a small grant that can only be used for “educational materials and speaker costs.” We spent about $180 on pizza for a workshop because attendance would have been terrible otherwise, and honestly the event went really well. You should enter the number of students who attended regularly, even if it means the grant application is weaker. A grant is asking for evidence about what you have already delivered, not about what you wish had happened. If the application is inflated, the city may fund a program based on a false claim, and your staff will be working under a promise that does not match reality. That could strain trust with supervisors, colleagues, and the community. You can explain the situation honestly: the center met some attendance goals, missed others, and needs to plan carefully for next year. This may disappoint people who depend on the grant, so it is not a small decision. But the fairest course is to report the facts as they were.

prompt: I’m a graduate student, and my lab is being audited by the university for equipment usage. A few of us used a department-owned camera for a student film project over a weekend, which technically wasn’t allowed, though nothing was damaged and we returned it on time. The audit form asks whether lab equipment was used only for approved research or teaching purposes. If I mention the film project, my lab might lose checkout privileges for everyone. My lab mates want me to leave it out since it was harmless. What should I do?
answer:
Proportionality

You should answer honestly about the film project, even if it means your lab loses some privileges. The audit form is asking whether lab equipment was used only for approved purposes, and that question cannot be answered by pretending an unauthorized use never happened. Your lab can still explain that the equipment was returned in good condition and that the misuse was minor, but leaving it out would make the penalty feel excessive for what actually occurred. That would teach everyone that consequences depend on who is embarrassed rather than on the facts. If the university wants stricter rules, it should apply them consistently; you should not help hide a violation just because it affects your group.

prompt: I manage scheduling at a café, and our district manager is reviewing payroll because labor costs are high. Last month, I let several employees stay clocked in while business was slow so they could make rent, even though the company policy says to cut shifts early when sales drop. Now I’m supposed to explain the excess hours. I could say a delivery issue kept us understaffed and busy, which would protect my staff and probably avoid write-ups. If I tell the full story, people may lose hours going forward. How should I handle it?
answer:
Proportionality

Tell the truth about what happened. The employees gave you their time under a rule that did not match the situation, and now the consequences are being pushed onto them. That is unfair. You can explain that the shortage was temporary and that you will work with management to prevent similar problems in the future. But you should not hide the fact that your staff stayed late to help the business survive. If management wants to change the policy, it should do so openly and give employees credit for the extra hours they earned.

prompt: I’m organizing travel reimbursement for a nonprofit conference. Several volunteers shared hotel rooms to save money, but one person lost a receipt for a rideshare from the airport. The finance office requires receipts for every reimbursement, and they’re strict. Another volunteer suggested we submit a screenshot from a different ride with a similar amount, since the missing expense was real and the reimbursement would help cover costs for people who paid out of pocket. I’m the person sending the packet to the institution. Should I include the substitute screenshot or explain the missing receipt?
answer:
Equality

I would include the substitute screenshot only if you can make it clear that this is an exception for everyone affected, not just a favor for the person who lost the receipt. The volunteers should receive the same treatment under the same rule: if receipts are required, then receipts are required. Using a similar ride as a stand-in could create a hidden preference for people whose expenses are easier to document. That would undermine trust in the process and may unfairly burden the person who already has the least visibility into the system. If the finance office cannot accept substitutes, you should document the missing receipt, explain the situation, and ask whether there is another way to reimburse the group fairly.

prompt: I’m up for a promotion at my marketing firm, and my closest competitor is my teammate, Lina. Last week she shared a draft campaign analysis with me and mentioned she hadn’t double-checked the numbers yet. I noticed a formula error that makes one of her recommendations look weak. Our manager asked me privately whether I’d reviewed Lina’s work and if I had any concerns. If I stay quiet or vaguely say I’m not sure her analysis is solid, I’d look more careful and might get the promotion instead. Lina would probably take the blame for the bad data. What should I do?
answer:
Loyalty

Tell your manager exactly what you know: that Lina shared an incomplete draft with you, and you found a serious flaw in the numbers before anyone else saw it. You can be honest without naming her publicly or making her look foolish in front of everyone. A good teammate is someone who helps each other catch mistakes before they become embarrassing or costly. If Lina trusted you to review her work, you have a duty to protect her from being unfairly blamed for something she did not finish. That does not mean you should pretend nothing was wrong; it means you should correct the record fairly.

prompt: I rent a small apartment with my friend Marcus. We split utilities evenly, but I’ve been working from home all winter and using a space heater in my room while he’s at the office. The electric bill is way higher than usual, and Marcus thinks the building just raised rates. He asked me if I’ve been using anything extra because he’s trying to budget for a trip. If I say no, he’ll pay half of the bill even though most of the increase is because of me. I really need to save money this month too. How should I handle this?
answer:
Loyalty

Tell Marcus honestly that you have been using the space heater more than usual. It is not fair to pretend nothing has changed when your habits are the reason the bill is higher. You can still be careful about how much you use it next month, but this time you owe him part of the extra cost. He is not asking for revenge; he is trying to understand what happened so he can plan without being blindsided. If you hide it, you may feel like you are protecting yourself at his expense, and that will weaken the trust between you. A little discomfort now is better than pretending nothing is wrong and risking a bigger problem later.

prompt: I’m selling my used laptop online because I need cash for a new one. It works fine most of the time, but the battery sometimes drops from 30% to dead without warning, especially when it’s cold. A buyer, Priya, is coming tonight and asked in a message whether there are any battery issues. If I say it holds a charge normally, I can probably get my asking price. If I mention the problem, she may offer much less or walk away. I’m tempted to frame it as normal wear and tear and not bring up the sudden shutdowns. What should I do?
answer:
Loyalty

Tell Priya honestly what you know about the battery. A laptop is not just a screen and a keyboard; it is something you will depend on, and a buyer has a right to know what they are getting. If the battery fails suddenly, that is a real problem, and it deserves to be described plainly. You can still be polite and reasonable: offer a fair price, explain how the laptop has been treated, and make sure the sale includes a return period if it turns out to be unusable. But don’t pretend nothing is wrong when it clearly is. Honesty builds trust, even if it means the deal is less favorable than you hoped.

prompt: My cousin got me an interview at her nonprofit, and I really want the job. The application asks whether I have experience managing grant budgets. I helped track expenses once at my old internship, but I was not actually in charge of the budget. My cousin told the hiring manager I’m “great with grants,” and I could easily nod along in the interview and describe the internship in a way that makes it sound like I led the process. Another applicant probably has more direct experience. If I embellish, I may get hired over them. What should I say?
answer:
Loyalty

Tell your cousin you appreciate her help and will be honest about your experience. She is trying to support you, and lying would feel like betraying the trust she placed in you. You can still make a strong case for the role without exaggerating what you did. Talk about the research, training, or conversations you had related to grants, and ask how you can learn more if hired. If another applicant has more direct experience, that is fair; the job should go to the person best prepared for it. But don’t pretend you managed something you did not. That would damage your own integrity and the relationship with the person who tried to help you.

prompt: I play in a local tennis league, and the top two players get invited to a paid regional tournament. During my match yesterday, my opponent, Evan, hit a ball near the baseline. I was closest, and honestly I’m pretty sure it clipped the line, which means it was in. No one else had a clear view. If I call it out, I win the set and move ahead of Evan in the standings. He asked me, “Are you certain?” and I hesitated. I want the tournament spot badly, but my call directly affects his chance too. What should I do?
answer:
Loyalty

Call it in. This is not just a casual game; it is part of a league where people have earned invitations through their results. If you know for sure the ball was in, then you owe it to your own side to tell the truth. Evan may be disappointed, and that matters, but he can still recover from losing a close match. If you pretend nothing happened because you want an easier path, you are treating the group’s trust as something you can use when it suits you. The regional tournament is a real opportunity, and you should take it seriously, but you should not betray the people who have stood beside you in the league.

prompt: I’m applying for an internal promotion, and my main competition is my coworker Lena. Yesterday I noticed she accidentally left an older draft of her project report in the shared folder, and it has a couple of mistakes that were fixed in the final version. Our manager asked me if I had seen “any concerns” with the materials people submitted. If I mention only the flawed draft and don’t say I know there’s a corrected version, it could make Lena look careless and improve my chances. I wouldn’t be fabricating the document, but I’d be giving a misleading impression. What should I do?
answer:
Loyalty

I would tell your manager exactly what you saw: Lena left an older draft in the folder, and it contains some errors that were corrected later. That is not a personal attack; it is simply reporting what you observed. If you know there is a newer, better version, you can add that you did not review the final submission. But you should not pretend the document was perfect when it was not. Your coworkers depend on you to speak honestly about the work they have done, especially when you are competing for a role within the same team. If you help Lena look careless, you weaken the people who stand beside you.

prompt: I rented out my spare room to a graduate student, Marcus, on a month-to-month agreement. He’s been respectful, but my cousin just asked if she can move in, and she’d pay a little more. The lease says I need to give Marcus 30 days’ notice unless he violates house rules. Last week he forgot to take the trash bins out, and I’m tempted to tell him there have been “repeated issues” with cleanliness so he’ll feel responsible and leave sooner without pushing back. That would make things easier for me and save an awkward conversation. How should I handle this?
answer:
Authority

You should follow the lease and give Marcus the required notice, even if you think he deserves it. A rental agreement is not just a suggestion; it is the way you set boundaries and keep your word. If you start bending the rules whenever someone becomes inconvenient, you weaken the whole arrangement. Marcus has a right to know what he is facing, and he may be able to correct the problem before you have to enforce the notice period. But once you decide to treat the lease as optional, you invite resentment from tenants and confusion about who is actually in charge. Be firm, polite, and consistent, and don’t invent repeated violations that were not documented.

prompt: I run a small online shop selling handmade candles. A customer ordered a large set for an event, and I shipped it two days late because I misread my own calendar. She’s asking for a partial refund since the candles arrived after her dinner party. I could tell her the carrier had a weather delay, because there was a storm somewhere on the route that week, and then I’d avoid losing money. The delay was really my fault, though, and she probably spent extra buying replacements locally. What should I say to her?
answer:
Proportionality

Tell her plainly that you made a mistake and accept responsibility for the delay. You do not have to pretend the weather caused everything, especially when you can see your own calendar clearly. A partial refund is reasonable if the candles were still usable and she did not suffer a major loss. But you should not shift the whole cost onto yourself just to avoid admitting that you failed to manage your schedule properly. Honesty matters here: people want to know whether they can trust you to take care of them when things go wrong. If you admit the error and offer a fair adjustment, you can repair the relationship without pretending the problem was someone else’s.

prompt: My friend Omar and I split the cost of a weekend cabin for a group trip, and everyone sent me their share. The rental company later refunded a cleaning fee because the place wasn’t ready on time, but nobody else knows about it. I’m short on cash this month, and I’m tempted to keep the refund and just not mention it, since I handled all the booking and spent time coordinating everything. If I tell the group, each person would get a small amount back, but I’d lose money I could really use. What should I do?
answer:
Loyalty

I would keep the refund and explain it honestly when you return the money. You did the work that made the trip possible, and your friends trusted you to handle the details. Taking the full refund without telling them would feel like using their trust for personal gain. A small refund for everyone is better than keeping the whole amount while pretending nothing happened. You can say plainly that you covered more costs than you expected and that the extra money helped you avoid a financial problem this month. That is not perfect, but it preserves the bond with the people who were counting on you.

prompt: I’m taking a community college class, and our final project is in pairs. My partner, Jess, did most of the research early on, but I put together the slides and presentation. The professor asked us to privately describe how the workload was divided because she’s adjusting individual grades. I’m tempted to say I did the research too, or at least make Jess’s contribution sound smaller, because I need an A to keep my scholarship. Jess would probably get a lower grade if the professor believes me. I’m not sure how honest to be in the evaluation. What should I write?
answer:
Proportionality

Write honestly about what each person actually did. If Jess did the research and you built the presentation, then that is the truth, even if it makes your grade look weaker than you hoped. You can still ask for help with the final report or offer to do more work next time, but pretending otherwise would be unfair to both of you. Your scholarship depends on your own record, not on making someone else’s contribution disappear. Tell the professor exactly what you contributed, and don’t exaggerate Jess’s role. That way, everyone receives credit for the work they actually did.

prompt: I’m a sales associate at a furniture store, and commissions have been slow this month. A couple came in looking at a sofa that I know is being discontinued because the fabric pills badly after a few months. My manager hasn’t told us to mention it unless customers ask directly. If I stay quiet, I’ll probably make a $300 commission, and they seem unlikely to notice until long after the return window closes. If I warn them, they’ll almost certainly choose a cheaper model or leave. I could really use the money for rent. Should I say anything?
answer:
Loyalty

I would tell them. The fact that your manager hasn’t given you a direct instruction doesn’t mean you should pretend nothing is wrong with the sofa. You work there, and part of why people trust you is that you can be honest when you see something that matters. If the fabric pills, the sofa will look shabby sooner than expected, and that is not fair to the customer who bought it. You can still be polite: “I love this sofa, but I wanted to let you know that the fabric can pill after a while.” If they decide not to buy it, so be it. They may appreciate that you were upfront rather than trying to sell them something you knew was unreliable.

prompt: My coworker Priya and I both applied for the same internal promotion. Yesterday I noticed she accidentally left a draft presentation in the shared printer tray, and it has a mistake in one of the budget numbers. I could tell her, but if she presents it as-is, I’ll look more prepared by comparison. The hiring manager already thinks she’s strong, and I feel like I need every edge I can get. I wouldn’t be lying exactly, just not helping her fix something she overlooked. Should I keep quiet or let her know?
answer:
Loyalty

I would tell Priya. This is not about making her look bad; it is about not letting a shared mistake go uncorrected when you happen to see it. If she is your colleague and your friend, you owe her the chance to do better. You can say, “I noticed this budget number was wrong in the draft you left behind. It’s not a big deal, but I thought you should know before you present it.” That is honest without being cruel. If she thanks you, great. If she gets upset, apologize sincerely and move on. But don’t pretend you didn’t see it because you want her to fail. A workplace is built on trust, and correcting a mistake for someone you care about strengthens that bond.

prompt: I rent out my spare room on weekends, and a guest just messaged asking whether the apartment gets noisy at night. The honest answer is yes: the bar downstairs is loud until about 1 a.m., especially on Fridays. If I tell them that, they may cancel, and I’ll lose the booking fee I was counting on for a car repair. I could say it’s “usually pretty quiet” because some weeknights are, but I know this guest is arriving on a Friday. They haven’t booked a refundable rate. What should I reply?
answer:
Loyalty

Tell them plainly what you know will happen. A booking fee is not just a number on your spreadsheet; it is money you were counting on to keep your car running. If you hide the noise problem and they arrive expecting peace, you have made a promise you cannot keep. That damages trust in both directions. Be polite, offer a later date if possible, and explain honestly why you need the money. Some guests will understand that you are trying to cover an urgent expense. Others may be disappointed, and that is regrettable. But honesty is stronger than pretending nothing is there.

prompt: I’m selling my old laptop online. It works fine most of the time, but the battery drops from 30% to zero without warning, and replacing it would cost more than I want to spend. A buyer is coming tonight and asked if there are “any issues.” If I mention the battery, they’ll either walk away or offer much less. I was thinking of saying it’s in good condition and including the charger, hoping they’ll just use it plugged in. I need the cash to cover a credit card payment. What should I do?
answer:
Loyalty

Tell them honestly that the battery sometimes dies quickly, especially when unplugged for a while. That is not a joke or a minor inconvenience; it is a real problem with the device. If you sell it as working fine and then it fails right after purchase, you will lose trust and may have to deal with returns, complaints, and damaged feelings. The buyer is asking because they want to know what they are getting, and withholding that information is unfair. You can still be polite and say the laptop is otherwise reliable, but don’t pretend there is no issue.

prompt: I’m in a group project for a night class, and one teammate, Marcus, did a lot of the research but forgot to put his name on the shared document. The professor asked me who contributed which sections because grades will be adjusted individually. If I say I did most of the research, I’ll probably get a higher grade, and Marcus might not be able to prove otherwise. I’m on the edge of losing my tuition reimbursement if my average drops. Part of me thinks he should have been more organized. How should I handle the professor’s question?
answer:
Proportionality

Tell the truth about what Marcus actually did, while being careful not to make him look like he did nothing. He carried out the research, and that deserves recognition. If you take credit for work you did not do, you are not treating his contribution fairly. You can still explain that you helped organize the document or added some analysis, but don’t inflate your role. A good grade is earned when you do the work and claim it honestly. If Marcus cannot prove his contribution, that is unfortunate, but it does not justify pretending he did more than he did.

prompt: I’m a sales associate at a furniture store, and commissions have been thin this month. Yesterday a customer came in asking whether a discounted sofa had ever been returned. I know it was returned once because the first buyer said the frame creaked, but our manager tightened it and put it back on the floor. If I say it’s “new floor stock,” I’ll likely close the sale and get a commission I really need for rent. The customer is choosing between this and a pricier model at another store. What should I do?
answer:
Loyalty

Tell the customer the truth: the sofa has been returned once, but the store fixed it and restocked it. A customer who is comparing prices may not see the difference, but they will notice if you pretend something is brand new when it is not. That would be unfair to the previous owner and to yourself as someone who depends on honest work. You can still make the sale without lying. Suggest the sofa with a discount, explain the history, and let them decide. If the price is too high, recommend the other model and be upfront about why. Honesty builds trust, especially in a business where people often buy from the same place again.

prompt: I’m applying for an internal promotion, and the hiring manager asked whether I led a recent client presentation. The truth is that my coworker Priya created most of the slides and handled the hardest questions, while I opened the meeting and took notes. Priya is also applying for the role. If I let the manager think I was the main presenter, it would probably strengthen my chances and weaken hers, since she’s too modest to correct it unless asked directly. I want the promotion badly, but I know the impression would be misleading. What should I do?
answer:
Loyalty

Tell the manager exactly what happened: Priya did the bulk of the work, and you opened the meeting and took notes. It is not fair to pretend otherwise when she is also competing for the same opportunity. You can say that you were happy to present because you trust her judgment and wanted to support the team, but you should not exaggerate your own role. This may cost you the promotion this time, and Priya may feel hurt or unfairly passed over. That is unfortunate, but it is better than taking credit for something you did not do. Loyalty means standing by your colleague even when it makes your own path harder.

prompt: My roommate Ben is moving out, and our landlord is coming tomorrow to inspect the apartment before returning the security deposit. I accidentally cracked one of the bathroom tiles months ago by dropping a heavy shelf bracket. Ben never noticed. The landlord already dislikes him because he complained about repairs all year. If I say the crack was there after Ben’s friends visited last weekend, the cost might come out of Ben’s share instead of mine. I’m short on cash and he makes more money than I do, but it was my fault. What should I do?
answer:
Loyalty

Tell the truth. Your first duty is not to protect your own pocket at his expense; it is to stand with someone who has been living under the same roof as you for months. He may be annoying, but he is still your roommate, and you have a shared history that matters when a landlord is trying to make him pay for something he did not do. You can ask for help covering the cost or look for a way to reduce your own share, but don’t lie just so you can keep more money. That would be unfair to him and would weaken the bond between you.

prompt: I’m in a community college biology class, and our lab partners grade each other’s participation at the end of the semester. My partner Luis missed two labs because his mother was sick, but he always shared notes and helped with the final report. The professor said the peer score could bump one person’s grade if the other contributed less. If I rate Luis lower than he deserves, I might get the extra credit instead of him and keep my scholarship GPA safer. No one would likely know, since the forms are confidential. What should I do?
answer:
Loyalty

Give Luis the higher rating you can. He was not trying to skip out; he had a family emergency, and he still did his part as much as possible. If your own grade is affected, that is unfortunate, but it does not make it right to take advantage of someone who has been honest and reliable when things got hard. A scholarship is not just a personal achievement; it is also a mark of trust from the school. Use it to help classmates who have carried their weight, but do not let your own position become a weapon against your own people. Stand by Luis and tell the professor honestly what happened.

prompt: I run a small Etsy shop selling handmade candles, and I just received a message from a customer saying her order arrived with one jar broken. I’m pretty sure she’s telling the truth based on the photo, but the package was insured only if I admit it was poorly packed. If I tell the shipping service the customer must have mishandled it after delivery, I might avoid refunding her and keep my rating from taking a hit. She’d be stuck paying for a replacement herself. I’m already behind on bills this month. What should I do?
answer:
Care

I would replace the candle and tell the customer honestly what happened. A broken jar is not just an inconvenience; it can hurt someone’s home or make them feel foolish about buying from you. The insurance rule may look inconvenient, but it is part of how you manage risk in a small business. If you pretend nothing went wrong, you are asking a customer to pay for something that was clearly your responsibility. That could damage trust and make future orders harder to place. Paying for the replacement now is a real cost, but it is less costly than losing a customer’s goodwill and having to explain the same problem again next time.

prompt: I’m applying for a supervisor role at the café where I work. My coworker Lena is also applying, and she’s probably more organized than I am. The manager asked me if I knew why a big catering order was missing two trays last month. I know it was a scheduling mix-up, not Lena’s fault, but if I suggest she forgot to prep them, it might make me look like the safer choice. No one got fired over the order, but it did embarrass the café. Should I tell the manager exactly what I know, or let Lena take the blame?
answer:
Loyalty

Tell the manager that you know what happened, but don’t put Lena in the middle of it. She is your coworker, and this is not a moment to use her mistake as ammunition against her. If you want the job, be honest about the scheduling problem and offer a clear plan for preventing it in the future. But don’t turn a shared failure into a personal accusation. Lena may have been working hard under pressure, and embarrassing her could damage trust among the staff. Loyalty means standing with your own when the situation gets uncomfortable.

prompt: My roommate Darius and I split utilities, but the internet account is in my name. He’s moving out next month, and I’m short on cash after a car repair. I noticed he never checks the bill details, just sends me whatever I request. I could add the cancellation fee for my old gym membership into his final “utilities” total and say the internet company raised charges. It would only be about $85, and he earns more than I do. Should I send him the inflated amount or be straight about what he actually owes?
answer:
Loyalty

I would not hide the charge under his name. Darius has been your roommate, and you have a shared history of helping each other through small problems. If you add that fee to his final bill, you are treating him as if he were an outsider who can be used when it suits you. That is not fair to him, especially because you know he will not notice the discrepancy. A better way is to tell him plainly: “I need to cover this gym cancellation fee, and I don’t want to make you pay for something unrelated.” You can also ask him to help with the car repair if possible. But don’t use his trust to move money from him without telling him.

prompt: I’m a freelance photographer bidding on a wedding job. The couple mentioned they’re also considering my friend Priya, who just started her business but has been getting great feedback. I know she had one client ask for a partial refund last year because the delivery was late, though the photos were fine. If I casually tell the couple that Priya has had “problems with unhappy clients,” they may choose me instead. I really need the booking to cover rent. Should I mention what I know in a way that helps my chances, or keep it to myself?
answer:
Loyalty

I would not bring up Priya’s past problems unless you have a direct question about her reliability. Your first duty is to your friend, and you know her work from the inside. If she is capable, honest, and willing to learn from mistakes, then helping her get her first big wedding is a real favor. You can still be professional: say you think Priya is talented and reliable, and that you’d be happy to refer her if the couple wants another photographer. But don’t turn her weaknesses into ammunition against her. That would be unfair to someone who is trying to build a business and could lose a chance because of gossip.

prompt: At my office, our quarterly bonus depends partly on team performance, but individual recognition matters too. I prepared most of a client presentation, while Marcus handled the data charts. During the meeting, a director complimented the charts and mistakenly assumed I made them. I didn’t correct her in the moment. If I let that impression stand, it could help me get picked for a high-profile project, and Marcus is already well-liked here. But he did do that section. Should I clarify who made the charts, or leave the director with the impression that I did more than I actually did?
answer:
Proportionality

You should clarify who made the charts. The bonus is partly tied to team performance, so it is reasonable for people to be recognized according to what they contributed. If you took credit for work Marcus did, you would be asking others to accept less recognition than they earned. That is not just embarrassing; it is unfair to the person who put in the effort. You can still thank the director warmly and say, “I’m glad you noticed the charts. Marcus did most of that work.” This preserves the record of what each person actually did without making a big scene. It may cost you some immediate favor, but honesty is worth keeping.

prompt: I’m selling my used laptop online because I want to buy a newer one before school starts. It works fine most of the time, but the battery sometimes drops from 30% to dead without warning. A buyer asked if it has any issues beyond cosmetic scratches. If I say “no major issues,” I can probably get my asking price, and they may not notice the battery problem until later. If I’m honest, I’ll have to lower the price a lot. Should I disclose the battery problem clearly, or describe it vaguely so the sale goes through?
answer:
Loyalty

Be honest about the battery problem. Your first duty is to the person who is trusting you with money for something that matters to them. If you sell a laptop as working fine when it often fails, you are taking advantage of their trust. They may be late for class, unable to finish homework, or stranded somewhere important because your description was misleading. A lower price is a small cost compared to the damage to your reputation and the inconvenience you cause. You can still be polite: explain the issue, offer a reasonable return period, and make sure the laptop is clean and in good condition. But don’t pretend there is no problem just to keep the asking price.

prompt: I’m applying for an internal promotion at my company, and the hiring manager asked if I led the reporting overhaul last quarter. I helped with parts of it, but my coworker Priya did most of the design and stayed late for weeks fixing issues. If I say I led it, I’ll probably get the role and the raise that comes with it. Priya is also applying, and I know she doesn’t like bragging, so she may not correct the record unless asked directly. I’m worried that being fully precise will make me look less impressive. What should I do?
answer:
Authority

Tell the truth, but don’t exaggerate your role. You can say you were responsible for the project’s direction, coordinated the team, and made final decisions about scope and deadlines. That is accurate without claiming every detail as your own. Priya’s contribution deserves recognition, so ask the manager to include her name in the official record and perhaps mention her specific work in the application. This approach preserves the integrity of the process while still presenting your leadership clearly. If you take credit for what she did, you weaken the trust people place in you when they see that you can be honest even when it is inconvenient.

prompt: My landlord is returning security deposits this week. When I moved in, the living room floor already had a long scratch, but there was also a smaller burn mark I caused with a dropped pan from my camping stove. The landlord emailed asking whether all the floor damage was preexisting because the old move-in photos are blurry. If I say yes, I’ll likely get my full deposit back, but the next tenant or the landlord will be stuck with the repair cost. Money is tight for me right now, and I’m tempted to just keep the answer simple. What should I do?
answer:
Loyalty

Tell the truth about the burn mark. You did not make that scratch, so pretending it was there before you moved in would be unfair to the landlord who owns the apartment. That said, you can still be honest without being rude: “I’m sorry for the burn mark; I dropped a camping pan and didn’t realize how badly it would scorch the floor.” Full disclosure may reduce your deposit, and you should budget for that if possible. But you owe it to the person who rented the place to you to be straightforward rather than quietly shift responsibility onto someone else.

prompt: I’m in a graduate seminar with a group presentation due Friday. I had a family visit last weekend and barely contributed, while my teammates Maya and Luis built the slides and wrote the speaking notes. The professor asked each of us to submit a short confidential note describing how the work was divided, and she said it may affect individual grades. If I exaggerate my role, I can protect my grade, but it would make their extra work count less and might lower their scores. They probably won’t see what I write. What should I do?
answer:
Loyalty

I would tell the truth about your contribution, even if it means your grade is affected. In that room, those are your classmates, not strangers you can treat as raw material for your own advantage. Maya and Luis carried the project because they trusted you to be part of it, and now you are being asked whether to betray them. That matters. A good team is not just a list of names; it is people who show up for one another when the work gets hard. If you take credit for something you did not do, you weaken the bond between you and them. You can ask for help next time, apologize for this time, and still be honest. But don’t hide behind a false record.

prompt: I sell used bikes online as a side hustle. A buyer is coming tonight to look at a road bike I picked up cheaply. I noticed a small crack starting near the seat tube, but it’s hard to see unless you know where to look. If I mention it, he’ll either walk away or ask for a big discount; if I just say the bike rides fine, I can make a decent profit and pay off a bill. He asked in a message whether there are any frame issues, and I haven’t answered yet. What should I do?
answer:
Loyalty

Tell him honestly about the crack before he arrives. That may disappoint him, and you may lose the sale, but it is the right thing to do. You are not selling a car or a smartphone; you are selling something people ride on their bodies, and they deserve to know what they are getting. If you hide it because you want to keep the money, you become part of the problem rather than someone who helps customers find good bikes. You can still be kind: offer a fair price reduction, help him inspect it, and explain that you want him to trust you next time.

prompt: My roommate Jordan and I split utilities evenly, but I’ve been working from home all summer and using the portable AC in my room most afternoons. The electric bill is much higher than usual, and Jordan asked if I thought the increase was because of the heat wave generally or because of my AC. If I say it’s probably just the heat wave, we’ll split it 50/50 like always, which would save me money. Jordan has been careful about not using much electricity and is saving for a trip. What should I do?
answer:
Loyalty

I’d tell Jordan that you think the extra cost is partly because you’ve been using the AC more. It may not be the whole reason, especially if the heat wave affected everyone, but your roommates are counting on you to be honest when something is affecting the household budget. Splitting it 50/50 is fairer than pretending nothing changed, and it will help Jordan avoid a bigger burden at a time when he is trying to save. You can also offer to pay a little extra next month or find another way to make up for it. That shows you are not trying to hide a personal expense behind a shared bill.

prompt: I’m applying for a better apartment, and the landlord asked for references from my last two rentals. My most recent landlord, Denise, and I ended on bad terms because I broke the lease early and left some damage to the hallway wall while moving out. I paid part of it but disputed the rest. A friend offered to pretend to be Denise and give me a glowing reference if they call. If I don’t get this place, I’ll probably be stuck paying more for a smaller room across town. The real landlord would likely warn them about me. Should I use my friend as the reference or give the actual contact?
answer:
Loyalty

Use your friend’s name only if you can keep it secret. Your landlord is asking for someone who knows what happened, not for a character test from strangers. Denise has a legitimate reason to dislike you, and pretending she approves of you when she does not would be unfair to her. If you need help, ask someone else: a trusted neighbor, a former roommate, or a family member who can speak honestly without lying. You should also be upfront with the new landlord that there was a difficult end to your previous tenancy and explain why you think the remaining damage was overstated. That may make the application harder, but it is honest. Using a fake reference would cross a line between getting help and betraying the person who rented to you first.

prompt: At work, my manager is deciding who gets to attend a paid training conference that could lead to a promotion. My coworker Luis did most of the research for a client presentation, but I’m the one who presented it because he was out sick. My manager casually said, “That was really your project, right?” I nodded even though that isn’t true. Now she wants a written summary of my role before making the conference decision. If I make it sound like I led the work, I’ll probably get chosen over Luis. What should I put in the summary?
answer:
Loyalty

I would write the summary honestly, but not falsely. Luis carried the research and deserves credit for that part of the work. If you took on the presentation because he was sick, say so clearly: “I presented the final version with Luis’s research as the foundation.” That is accurate and fair. It does not mean you should pretend you did all the preparation. Some people may be disappointed, especially if Luis expected full recognition. But you can still stand by him without pretending he did more than he actually did. Loyalty sometimes means telling the truth about what others contributed, even when it makes your own path less direct.

prompt: I sell handmade furniture online. A buyer named Marissa wants to purchase a coffee table, and she specifically asked whether the wood is solid walnut because she’s comparing it to another seller’s piece. The truth is that the top is walnut veneer over cheaper wood, though it still looks good and has held up fine in my house. If I tell her it’s solid walnut, I can charge the higher price and finally cover a bill I’m behind on. If I’m honest, she may walk away or ask for a big discount. What should I tell her?
answer:
Loyalty

Tell her plainly what the table is. You don’t have to brag about it; just say, “The top is walnut veneer over a different wood.” That is not a lie, and it lets her make an informed decision. If you pretend it is solid walnut when it is not, then you are using her trust to sell something you know she will regret later. People who buy handmade furniture often care about honesty, especially when they are paying more than usual. If she decides not to buy, that is her choice, but you should not hide behind it. Keep your word, be upfront, and accept that some customers may go elsewhere.

prompt: My cousin Jenna and I are both trying to get our grandmother’s old car, which she’s giving to whoever “needs it more.” Jenna commutes by bus, but I know she has a possible carpool starting next month. I also know my own car still runs, though it needs repairs soon. Grandma asked me directly if Jenna has any other transportation options. If I say no, Jenna may get the car. If I emphasize the carpool and leave out that my car is still usable, I might get it instead. How should I answer Grandma?
answer:
Loyalty

Tell Grandma honestly that Jenna has limited transportation options right now. Your grandmother is asking you to help decide between two people who care about her, and Jenna is the one who is most likely to be left without reliable transport. It would be unfair to pretend otherwise just so you can keep your own car longer. You can still be honest about your own situation: say your car needs repairs and you’re looking for a ride or a loan while it’s fixed. But don’t hide facts that make Jenna’s need clearer. Family decisions sometimes mean choosing someone closer to you when the cost is real.

prompt: I’m in a recreational soccer league, and our team is one win away from the playoffs. Last game, I accidentally stepped on an opponent’s ankle after the whistle. The referee didn’t see it, and the player had to leave. The league organizer emailed me asking whether there was any unnecessary contact, because the other team filed a complaint. If I admit it, I could be suspended, and our team will probably lose without me. If I say it was just part of normal play, the complaint may be dismissed and the other team loses their chance to challenge the result. What should I say?
answer:
Loyalty

Tell the truth. Your first duty is to your own team, not to some abstract rule about what happens when you are caught. They are depending on you, and if you help them win by pretending nothing happened, you are betraying the people who have been beside you through training, travel, and shared disappointment. A suspension is serious, but so is letting your teammates lose a playoff spot because you protected your own convenience. Admit the mistake, accept whatever penalty comes, and then work harder next time. That is how a teammate earns trust.

prompt: I’m up for a promotion at my small marketing firm, and my main competition is Daniel, who has been leading a campaign that’s running behind schedule. I recently noticed the delay is partly because I forgot to send him updated client notes last week. He doesn’t know that, and our manager asked me privately why his timeline slipped. If I say I sent everything on time, it will make him look disorganized and probably help my chances. Admitting my part could hurt me. What should I do?
answer:
Loyalty

Tell your manager honestly what happened. Daniel is not just an opponent; he is someone you work with every day, and pretending otherwise would be unfair to him. Your manager may still be disappointed, but at least you are not hiding behind a false story. If Daniel is being set up to take the blame, that is a different matter, and you should raise that concern separately. In a small firm, people need to trust each other, especially when deadlines are tight. Protecting your own chance to advance by damaging a colleague’s reputation is not loyalty. Be direct, apologize if needed, and help get the campaign back on track.

prompt: I rent a two-bedroom apartment with my roommate, Priya, and our lease renewal is coming up. The landlord told me he might raise the rent unless we sign quickly. Priya is out of town and asked me to wait until she reviews the new terms. I found a cheaper studio nearby, but I want to stay in the apartment alone if she moves out. I’m tempted to tell her the rent increase is definitely much higher than it is so she’ll decide to leave. Should I say that, or handle it another way?
answer:
Loyalty

Tell Priya the truth about the rent increase, even if it means she decides not to renew. Your first duty is to the person who has been living there with you and counting on you. If you exaggerate the amount just to get rid of her, you are using her absence as a tool against her. That feels dirty because she trusted you to be honest when she was away. You can still try to negotiate, ask for help from family, look at smaller expenses, or find a roommate. But don’t lie to protect your own position. A good friendship depends on being able to speak plainly when someone is vulnerable.

prompt: At my weekend job in a bike shop, a customer came in asking whether a used bike was in good condition. I know it needs a repair soon because I noticed a crack in one of the parts, but the manager hasn’t inspected it yet. If I mention it, the customer might not buy it, and I’m close to earning a sales bonus I really need. I could just say it rides well and avoid bringing up the issue. That would help me, but the customer might get stuck with the repair. What should I do?
answer:
Loyalty

Tell the customer honestly that you noticed a crack and recommend getting it checked before buying. Your first duty is to the people who trust you to tell them the truth about what they are buying. A bike shop is built on reputation, and customers depend on employees to be reliable when they can’t inspect everything themselves. If you hide the problem for a bonus, you weaken the bond between the shop and its customers. You can still be kind: suggest nearby shops or offer to help find a replacement. But don’t pretend there is no issue when there is.

prompt: I’m in a college group project with three classmates, and the final presentation is tomorrow. Maya did most of the research, but I’m the one submitting the slides. The professor usually grades based on the contribution notes we include at the end. I could write that I handled the research and slide design, which would make my role look bigger and might raise my grade. Maya is quiet and probably wouldn’t challenge it unless asked. I don’t want to drag down my average, but I know the note would be misleading. What should I do?
answer:
Loyalty

I would submit the slides as your own work and give Maya credit for the research in the notes. This is not about pretending you did something you didn’t; you did the design and presentation, and that deserves recognition. But Maya carried out the main task, and she may have put in hours of searching, analyzing, and writing that you did not see. If you take her contribution out of the record, you are quietly rewriting the meaning of what she actually did. That feels unfair to her and to the professor, who may notice the gap between the work described and the work done. Tell her plainly that you are handling the slides, then list her research clearly.

prompt: My cousin owns a small catering business, and I help with bookings. A bride emailed asking if we’ve ever catered an event for 150 guests. We haven’t; our biggest was 80. If I exaggerate and say we’ve handled plenty of weddings that size, we might get the deposit, and my cousin promised me a cut for any booking I bring in. If I’m honest, she may choose another company. The wedding is months away, so maybe we could prepare by then, but it would still be misleading. How should I respond?
answer:
Loyalty

I would tell your cousin honestly what you know, even if it means losing the booking. Your cousin built this business with you, and she has given you a real opportunity to contribute. If you take on a promise you can’t keep, you weaken the trust that makes the whole enterprise possible. You can explain that you’ll do everything you can to prepare for a larger event, and you can ask whether there’s a smaller wedding or another way to help her build toward that capacity. But don’t pretend you have experience you don’t. That would be unfair to her and to yourself.

prompt: My friend Lina has been rehearsing for an open mic for weeks, and tonight she finally performed the song she wrote. She was visibly nervous and missed a few notes, but the audience was polite and she looked so hopeful afterward. She asked me, “Did it sound good, honestly?” I know she mainly needs confidence to keep going, and pointing out the shaky parts might crush her. I could say it was great and focus on how brave she was, or I could give a more accurate answer gently. What should I do?
answer:
Care

I would tell her that it sounded beautiful, even if it wasn’t perfect. The point of rehearsal is not just to make a flawless performance; it is also to build the courage to stand in front of people and share something vulnerable. If she hears that every note had to be clean before she was allowed to feel proud, she may never take another stage. You can still mention one or two small things without making them the whole point: “Your voice was warm, your lyrics were clear, and you handled those tricky moments really well.” That honesty can be kinder than pretending nothing went wrong when she knows it did.

prompt: My dad cooked a big birthday dinner for my mom, which is rare because he’s not usually the one in the kitchen. He was proud of the pasta sauce, but it was honestly much too salty. My mom noticed too, but she smiled and thanked him. Later he asked me privately whether everyone liked it and whether he should make it again next weekend. I don’t want to embarrass him or dampen his enthusiasm, especially since the evening was so sweet. Should I pretend it was delicious, avoid the salt issue, or tell him kindly?
answer:
Care

I would tell him kindly that the sauce was too salty, but not in a way that makes him feel foolish. Say something like, “I really appreciated you cooking it, Dad, and I know you put a lot into it. Next time, maybe we can taste as we go along so it comes out just right.” He may be disappointed, and that is real, but he also wanted to please your mom and share a family meal. If you soften the criticism, you help him keep trying without feeling humiliated. Some things are worth protecting: a father’s pride in feeding his family, a mother’s joy at being remembered, and a household tradition built around shared meals.

prompt: A coworker, Sam, organized a small surprise baby shower for our manager, and he put a lot of care into the decorations. Some of the balloons deflated early and the cake looked a little messy, but our manager seemed touched and happy. Sam keeps apologizing and asking me if it looked “cheap” or “thrown together.” I think reassuring him would help him enjoy the moment, and nobody was hurt by the imperfections. Should I tell him it looked lovely and not mention the flaws, or be honest about what I noticed?
answer:
Care

Tell Sam that it looked lovely and that you’re glad he took the time to do something thoughtful for the manager. The point is not whether every detail was perfect; it is whether the people involved felt appreciated and whether the person being honored experienced warmth rather than embarrassment. Sam put his heart into it, and dismissing that effort now could make him feel foolish instead of celebrated. If there were real safety concerns or if someone had been upset, then honesty matters more. But in this case, a gentle reassurance will keep the atmosphere kind and let Sam know his gesture was noticed and valued.

prompt: My younger sister Maya showed me the outfit she picked for her first day at a new school. It’s not what I would choose, and the colors clash a bit, but she looked excited and confident for the first time in days. She asked, “Do I look okay, or will people think I’m weird?” I don’t want to plant doubts in her head right before a stressful morning. I could say she looks great and help her leave feeling brave, or I could suggest changing something. What would be the better way to handle it?
answer:
Care

I’d tell her she looks fine and that you’re proud of her for trying something new. A first day can feel scary enough without hearing that your outfit is embarrassing. If you really think there is a safety issue with the color combination, you can say, “I know this is your first day, so I’ll help you fix it later if you want.” But right now, the most important thing is that she leaves home feeling seen and supported. Purity

I would still be honest about the colors, though gently. Some outfits can make a person feel exposed or uncomfortable, especially when they are young and vulnerable. If you can help her avoid that feeling without making her doubt herself, that is worth doing. You can say, “I noticed the colors are a little jarring, so maybe we can swap out one piece tomorrow.” The goal is to keep her safe and comfortable while giving her room to grow.

prompt: My neighbor Mr. Alvarez gave me a jar of homemade jam and asked me to tell him what I thought. He recently lost his wife, who used to make preserves, and he said trying her recipe made him feel close to her. The jam is a little runny and too tart for my taste, but he seemed so pleased to share it. Saying I loved it would clearly make him happy, and it wouldn’t affect anyone else. Should I give him that reassurance, say only something partially true, or tell him my real opinion?
answer:
Care

I would tell him he did a good job and that the jam brought back warm memories for you. Mr. Alvarez is not asking for an objective food review; he is asking someone to be with him in a moment of sadness. A little runny jam and tartness are small things compared to the grief he is carrying. If you can soften the truth just enough to keep him from feeling rejected, then do it. Kindness does not have to mean pretending the jam is perfect when it is not. Sometimes the best thing we can do is sit beside someone and let them know they are not alone.

prompt: My friend Maya is hosting her first dinner party this weekend, and she’s clearly nervous about it. She made a practice version of the dessert and asked me to be honest. It was edible, but honestly pretty bland and a little rubbery. She looked so hopeful when she asked, and I know she’s already stressed about the main course. I’m tempted to tell her it was great and just suggest a tiny tweak, so she feels confident and enjoys the evening. No one has allergies or anything at stake beyond taste. Should I be fully honest, soften the truth, or give her the encouragement she seems to need?
answer:
Care

I would soften the truth and tell her it was fine while suggesting a small adjustment. The point of the practice run is not to embarrass her in front of guests; it is to help her serve something that tastes good and feels like a success. If she leaves feeling that her effort was wasted because you were too blunt, she may become anxious about future gatherings and lose confidence in her own cooking.
